Place's $4M Westbury Avenue project to bring new sidewalks, street repaving","teaserTitle":"Town's $4M revitalization project begins","body":"\u003cp\u003eNorth Hempstead Town began work on the\u0026nbsp;long-awaited\u0026nbsp;reconstruction and beautification of Westbury Avenue in Carle Place on Tuesday morning.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe project will transform the hamlet's main thoroughfare into\u0026nbsp;\"a better heartbeat for the community of Carle Place,\" Supervisor Jennifer DeSena said during an on-site news\u0026nbsp;conference Tuesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe approximately $4 million project will be funded by $2.5 million from Nassau County, which manages the roadway, and\u0026nbsp;$1 million from the\u0026nbsp;federal American Rescue Plan Act. The rest is coming from the town.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe work, to be done by the Hicksville-based contractor Stasi General Contracting, will include sidewalk replacements, street repaving, curb improvements, drainage updates and improved pedestrian crossings for a nearly mile-long stretch of the road from Jamaica Boulevard to Carle Road.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We're rebuilding a road, but that's not the big picture. What we're really building here is a better Westbury Avenue,\" DeSena said. \"We're constructing a safer, more attractive 'Main Street' for the people who live here, work here\u0026nbsp;and visit here.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDeSena added: \"We're making a more welcome environment for the businesses that call Carle Place home.\"\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePlans for the revitalization date back two decades\u0026nbsp;but have long stalled amid bureaucratic challenges, DeSena said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"When you have many layers of government, sometimes they point the finger at each other,\" she said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCouncilman Robert Troiano, who represents Carle Place,\u0026nbsp;said during the news\u0026nbsp;conference that the project would\u0026nbsp;help \"rebuild pride in the Carle Place community for their Westbury Avenue.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"This is a community that takes great pride in its schools ... and its homes,\" Troiano said. \"They are connected, in every way possible. But they've never been quite so proud about their downtown.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLast year, Troiano notified town code enforcement officials of overgrown weeds in the right of way of several storefronts and office buildings on Westbury Avenue.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn an interview,\u0026nbsp;Troiano said\u0026nbsp;the project should be complete\u0026nbsp;by May.\u0026nbsp;A town news release said residents should expect \"occasional lane closures, alternating traffic patterns, temporary detours, and some parking restrictions in the project area.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDominick D'Alonzo, president of the Carle Place Civic Association, told Newsday\u0026nbsp;the \"long overdue\" project would\u0026nbsp;be a boon for the village's small businesses.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It's tough to be a small business in this day and age, and then with COVID, everyone took a hit,\" he said. \"Now, we're starting to get a rebirth.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEric Alexander, director of Vision Long Island, a\u0026nbsp;downtown planning organization, said in an interview the improvements would\u0026nbsp;help walkability in the village,\u0026nbsp;which would\u0026nbsp;help with pedestrian safety and make for a more bustling downtown.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe project represents a\u0026nbsp;\"positive example of pedestrian improvements in communities across Long Island. We need many more,\" he said. He added community members had\u0026nbsp;been pushing for the ability to \"walk into town or park and walk safely, frequent the stores.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe town has undertaken several infrastructure improvements in recent months, including the replacement of the Webster Avenue Bridge and a shoreline stabilization project along Bayview Avenue in Manhasset.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/0292736c-b0f1-4ca6-aee9-38987e8de9b6","title":"AIAudio - educator salaries: 8 of the 10 highest-paid educators in 2025-26 worked in Long Island schools","teaserTitle":"8 of the 10 highest-paid educators in NYS work in LI schools","body":"\u003cp\u003eEight of the 10 highest-paid public school educators in the state worked on Long Island in the 2025-26 school year, with Roslyn’s superintendent topping the list, a Newsday analysis found.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe veteran educator, Allison Brown, received a pay package of $436,975, which included her base salary and unspecified additional pay, according to state data. The second-highest-paid educator was Great Neck schools Superintendent Kenneth Bossert, who earned a total of\u0026nbsp;$420,781.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe 10 highest earners in K-12 schools statewide were all administrators, including nine superintendents and one deputy superintendent. In addition to Bossert, the Great Neck school district had a second administrator in the top 10 — Deputy Superintendent John O'Keefe, with total pay of $375,210.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPAY261122_ chart\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFinancial watchdog groups have questioned whether that money should instead be used elsewhere in the school system, and\u0026nbsp;to\u0026nbsp;achieve better academic outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The fact that essentially a bureaucrat and manager is making that type of money is just a negative side effect of bureaucracy,” said Zilvinas Silenas, president of the Empire Center for Public Policy, a conservative-leaning think tank based in Albany.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Why isn't that money put into achieving better results?” he added. “Why isn't this money put into classrooms?”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut supporters have argued competitive compensation packages attract and retain the talent needed to manage schools that will educate the next generation of doctors, electricians and chief executives. They also pointed to the high cost of living on the Island, where homeowners pay among the highest property taxes in the country.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAbout two-thirds of a homeowner's property taxes generally go to fund schools, with payroll\u0026nbsp;the single largest expense for districts.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRobert Lowry, senior education finance and policy analyst at the New York State Council of School Superintendents, said superintendents have a wide range of responsibilities, from high-level decision-making over safety and instruction down to whether the cafeteria has enough healthy food options.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLowry also noted home values are often tied to the quality of the school district.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The question becomes,\u0026nbsp;‘How much is all that worth to you?’ ” he said. “Don't you want to make sure that you have a professional leader of your school system who's up to dealing with all those things?”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eTotal pay on LI nears $6.5 billion\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday's analysis was based on figures obtained from the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System through a Freedom of Information Law request. The annual payroll data covers\u0026nbsp;teachers, administrators, guidance counselors and other staffers who worked in the state’s public schools in 2025-26. It also includes some employees of SUNY colleges. New York City schools\u0026nbsp;employees were excluded from the database.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe combined compensation for more than 264,000 educators across New York topped $20 billion last school year, the state data shows. On the Island,\u0026nbsp;total pay for about\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003e68,000 employees neared $6.5 billion.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPAY261122_html_table\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn the 2025-26 academic year, 79 K-12 and SUNY employees on the Island earned more than $300,000, up from 64 a year prior. Another 1,317 made between $200,000 and $300,000 last school year, up from 1,129 in 2024-25, according to the data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhile SUNY employees were included in the database, Newsday excluded them from the top 10 ranking because\u0026nbsp;salary levels in the statewide university network are not comparable to those set by local school boards.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIsland schools chiefs who appeared on the top earners list also include:\u0026nbsp;Francesco Ianni, of Oyster Bay-East Norwich, who received\u0026nbsp;$412,662;\u0026nbsp;Kathleen Bannon in Copiague, with a $389,246\u0026nbsp;pay package;\u0026nbsp;Kevin Scanlon, of\u0026nbsp;Three Village, with $376,761; Joseph Famularo at Bellmore with $375,771; and Kevin Coster, of William Floyd, with $365,206.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTwo additional administrators — interim Webutuck Central schools Superintendent Raymond Castellani\u0026nbsp;in Dutchess County and Amy Creeden, superintendent of Middletown schools — also were on the list. They made $389,356 and $376,701 respectively.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday reached out to all 10 administrators and their respective school board presidents. They either declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment. Five districts responded with statements and two noted their superintendents'\u0026nbsp;long tenure as reasons contributing to\u0026nbsp;their pay.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Roslyn, Brown’s base salary for 2025-26 was $363,262. District spokeswoman Cynthia Younker did not say what made up the superintendent’s remaining pay of more than $70,000, but she\u0026nbsp;noted Brown is in her 11th year\u0026nbsp;as superintendent after first joining the district in 2008.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOver nearly two decades in the district, Brown has worked her way up through the ranks, from a principal to an assistant superintendent and later deputy superintendent, according to her biography posted on the district website.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe 3,300-student Nassau district was recently\u0026nbsp;\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/niche-rankings-long-island-school-districts-idkfwe8r\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eranked by Niche as the second-best district\u003c/a\u003e in the country.\u003cspan style=\"background-color: rgba(255, 255, 0, 0.3);\"\u003e \u003c/span\u003eRoslyn High School has consistently \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/regeneron-science-talent-search-long-island-ccm8htc8\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eproduced semifinalists\u003c/a\u003e in the prestigious Regeneron competition and\u0026nbsp;students in the district have won\u0026nbsp;awards ranging from the region’s math fair to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/li-life/roslyn-student-npr-podcast-challenge-yz8zb4h0\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eNPR's Podcast Challenge\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLeonardo Nunez Botto, of Flower Hill, believes Brown’s pay was excessive, especially when compared with other districts: “I think it's quite too much money for the superintendent.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca Botto told Newsday he thinks the Roslyn schools superintendent's salary is excessive.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePat Goldstein, of East Hills, however, said she didn’t have an issue with it as long as the district was willing to pay it. Goldstein’s two adult children graduated from Roslyn schools in 2009 and 2013 and she considered the district to have provided a good education to them.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“I was always satisfied with the programs that they had,” she said. “If they can get it, why not? I'm not going to begrudge them.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Pat Goldstein, meanwhile, was happy with the education her adult children received in the Roslyn school district.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7/liPAY261122c.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003ePat Goldstein, meanwhile, was happy with the education her adult children received in the Roslyn school district.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eExperience, academic outcomes cited\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen asked for comment about the superintendent's pay, William Floyd district spokesman\u0026nbsp;James Montalto cited rising graduation rates under Coster’s tenure and his three decades of experience in education.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMontalto also pointed to the district’s size. William Floyd is one of the Island’s biggest districts with 9,500 students, 1,500 staffers and a budget of $332 million.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Since assuming the role in 2015, the district’s graduation rate has increased from 79% to 95%, alongside significant improvements in facilities, an upgrade in the district’s bond rating and expanded educational opportunities in Career and Technical Education, science, music, the arts, athletics, and more,” Montalto wrote in an email.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMontalto said Coster’s base salary for 2025-26 was $325,485 and the additional pay of nearly $40,000 came from a\u0026nbsp;payout for unused sick and vacation time at the end of last school year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWanda Ortiz-Rivera, superintendent of the Island’s largest school district in Brentwood, which serves\u0026nbsp;18,000 students, earned\u0026nbsp;$295,155 last school year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThree Village\u0026nbsp;spokeswoman Denise Nash noted\u0026nbsp;the superintendent's\u0026nbsp;pay figure includes other compensation in addition to\u0026nbsp;Scanlon’s base pay.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThree Village was one of five Island districts that held a revote after residents rejected its initial budget proposal that called for a 4.54% tax levy hike. Voters later approved a lower increase.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnlike the other superintendents whose gross pay went up, Scanlon was the only one on the top earners list whose compensation stayed the same from 2024-25 to 2025-26.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Great Neck, a spokeswoman said the pay figures for Bossert and O'Keefe included\u0026nbsp;base pay and contractual benefits.\u0026nbsp;Bossert and O'Keefe could cash in unused vacation days, and O'Keefe was entitled to an annual “longevity” payment of $6,000, according to their contracts. Both had a car allowance: Bossert at $1,000 per month and O'Keefe at $500.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBossert is also serving as president of the New York State Council of School Superintendents this year.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eGreat Neck schools are \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/us-news-world-report-best-schools-nys-htwt8mik\" target=\"_blank\"\u003econsidered among the best\u003c/a\u003e in the state with \u003ca href=\"https://data.nysed.gov/essa.php?instid=800000049062\u0026amp;year=2025\u0026amp;createreport=1\u0026amp;HSgradrate=1\u0026amp;38ELA=1\u0026amp;38MATH=1\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ehigh graduation rates and proficiency levels\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Copiague, a statement from the district said the superintendent's\u0026nbsp;compensation “reflects salary, contractual benefits and payouts for earned but unused sick leave and vacation days in accordance with the terms of Dr. Bannon’s employment agreement.”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBannon has led the district \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/copiague-s-superintendent-to-retire-in-august-and-be-replaced-by-associate-superintendent-x93935\" target=\"_blank\"\u003esince 2015\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBettianne Balzano, who has lived in Copiague for 27 years, said she found Bannon’s total pay to be “ludicrous.”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“It's unfortunate because I think that our taxes are so exorbitant,” she said. “And it's a shame. We live in a beautiful place and I love it here. But a lot of people are being taxed out of here.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Bettianne Balzano took issue with the superintendent's compensation.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31/DEC_6648.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eBettianne Balzano took issue with the superintendent's compensation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJessica Dejesus, a mother of two, took a different view.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDejesus said she had moved from Brooklyn to Long Island for a better life for her children and she has been pleased with the education her two kids, 9 and 16, received from the Copiague district.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“I really do feel like it is a better life out here,” she said. “The taxes for me personally, I can't speak [for] everyone else, is worth it for my kids to have a better life. Island town and city healthcare premiums climb to $344M, triggering tax hikes","teaserTitle":"'Skyrocket out of control': LI town, city healthcare costs rise to $344M","body":"\u003cp\u003eLong Island towns and cities spent $344.4 million on employee and retiree healthcare premiums last year, a ballooning cost that officials say is expected to trigger\u0026nbsp;tax hikes and further strain municipal budgets.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe total across Long Island's 13 towns and two cities was up about 3% over 2024, and 37% over 2021, according to state data analyzed by Newsday. Municipal officials, facing a Nov. 20 deadline to finalize 2027 spending plans, expect\u0026nbsp;the cost to rise steeply\u0026nbsp;next year.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: Change in employee, retiree health insurance costs \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOfficials have cited the sharply rising expense of covering employee and retiree\u0026nbsp;healthcare plans as a key driver of annual tax hikes. The benefit can account for more than 15% of some town and city spending plans, making it among their largest single expenses.\u0026nbsp;State-set premiums\u0026nbsp;have risen an average of 6% annually since 2021 and increased\u0026nbsp;nearly 10% in 2026, the highest change in years, state data shows.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHealthcare costs between 2024 and\u0026nbsp;2025\u0026nbsp;rose the most in\u0026nbsp;Long Beach, where the city experienced a 17%, or $2.6 million, jump\u0026nbsp;to $17.6 million. In the Town of Oyster Bay, the expense rose\u0026nbsp;nearly 19%, or $7.1 million, to $45.1 million.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It's unlike almost anything else on our budget,\" Rob Darienzo, Oyster Bay's budget director, said in an interview. \"We do our best to keep our salaries the same, and we try to reduce our debt. And yet, the health insurance premiums, mandated by New York State, they skyrocket out of control.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBudget officials are bracing for \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/town-city-village-pension-spending-tnzljx37\"\u003edouble-digit-percent increases\u003c/a\u003e to healthcare expenses each year,\u0026nbsp;on top of surging employee pension costs. The increases have compelled towns and cities to keep their workforces flat and lean on incentive programs to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/riverhead-employee-retirement-incentive-dla3b8eg\"\u003ereduce the number of highly paid workers\u003c/a\u003e and the cost\u0026nbsp;of their benefits, officials said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNearly 7,000 town and city employees\u0026nbsp;are covered by the New York State Health Insurance Plan. NYSHIP covers about 27,000 dependents on Long Island,\u0026nbsp;according to the\u0026nbsp;state Department of Civil Service, which administers the health plan.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNYSHIP premium rates, which are set by the state, rose\u0026nbsp;2.2% in 2021, 7.4% in 2022, 8.6% in 2023 and 8.9% in 2024 but were flat in 2025, the agency said. Then, in 2026, premium rates jumped\u0026nbsp;9.6%.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: NYSHIP annual rate increases \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe\u0026nbsp;rate changes are affected by several factors, officials say, from the\u0026nbsp;number of employees enrolled in family plans to\u0026nbsp;increases in\u0026nbsp;the cost of medical procedures.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe rising burden of funding benefit programs\u0026nbsp;is a \"huge problem\" in the long term, said\u0026nbsp;Zilvinas Silenas, president of the\u0026nbsp;Empire Center, a conservative think tank based in Albany.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"If this continues, meaning more and more people claim benefits or the benefits become increasingly generous or even the wages become more generous, there is a finite number of taxpayers in New York that can support that,\"\u0026nbsp;Silenas said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eClimbing costs\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHealthcare costs, along with other annual increases like contractual raises and retirement benefits, make it difficult to stay below the state's 2% tax cap, Southampton Supervisor Maria Moore said. Last year, the town negotiated for\u0026nbsp;new employees to pay 15% of their healthcare benefits, rather than 10%, to help blunt the rising cost\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003eas part of its contract with the Civil Service Employees Association union.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: LI town and city healthcare costs \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"How can you stay below 2% when just the salary increases contractually are 3%, the healthcare is going up 6% more than likely, the pension will likely go up another 10% ... not to mention the cost of gas, diesel [and] materials?\" Moore said. \"Everything costs more now.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSouthampton's healthcare costs\u0026nbsp;have risen from\u0026nbsp;$17 million in 2022 to $22.1 million in 2025, state data shows.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBabylon Deputy Comptroller Cathy Wuertz said governments are in a defensive position\u0026nbsp;while preparing\u0026nbsp;budgets.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We budget conservatively,\" Wuertz said. \"Some years it works in our favor, where we get a couple of bucks that we didn’t have to spend. You budget according to what you think is going to happen, according to trends, and you just go from there.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eFuture concerns\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"North Hempstead Town Hall. The town's healthcare costs are forecast to jump even more next year.\n\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-f=\"3x2\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83/TOWNHALLS2257782689100506.jpg?f=3x2\u0026amp;w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eNorth Hempstead Town Hall. The town's healthcare costs are forecast to jump even more next year. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe tide of rising healthcare costs isn't expected to recede in the near future, officials said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEast Hampton's 2027 budget anticipated $14.8 million in health insurance costs, a nearly 5% increase over this year.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe state usually releases its official rate increases in late November or December\u0026nbsp;— after town and city budgets are finalized. That means officials\u0026nbsp;base budgets, and project one of their largest expenses,\u0026nbsp;off\u0026nbsp;limited information.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"A lot of that is really just trying to, for lack of a better phrase, sharpening your pencils — looking at prior year history and increases, and really just hoping that you're coming up with as best of an accurate number as possible,\" East Hampton Town Administrator Rebecca Hansen said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOn the national level, healthcare premiums have risen at a fast clip, as more patients sign up for\u0026nbsp;mental health services and undergo\u0026nbsp;expensive treatments,\u0026nbsp;said Matthew Rae, associate director for the healthcare marketplace program at KFF, a Washington, D.C., health policy and research nonprofit. Newer drugs on the market, like GLP-1s and emerging cancer treatments, are also driving premium hikes, Rae said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat leaves employers to shoulder a growing expense.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"What used to be considered an expensive drug was $100,000. There are now a lot of drugs on the market that are $1 million,\" Rae said, referring to treatments for cancers and diseases like sickle cell. \"How we finance that may be a challenge, and for whatever reason we made employers the basis of our healthcare finance system, but we need to figure out how to pay for stuff like that that\u0026nbsp;is remarkably changing people's lives.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn North Hempstead, healthcare costs rose nearly 2% between 2025 and 2026 but\u0026nbsp;are expected to rise almost 6% next year, said Umberto Mignardi, a town spokesman.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCosts have climbed due to \"higher medical facility and physician fees, rising specialty drug and prescription costs, aging active and retiree plan demographics, state-mandated coverage expansions and caps on member out-of-pocket spending,\" Mignardi said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eCreative decisions\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Smithtown Town Hall. The town eliminated more than 30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025. \n\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-f=\"3x2\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018/TOWNHALLS05914156.jpg?f=3x2\u0026amp;w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eSmithtown Town Hall. The town eliminated more than 30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome towns\u0026nbsp;have resorted to workforce reductions and buyouts to keep pace.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn October, Suffolk County \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/tax-cap-suffolk-supervisors-tavmen4v\"\u003esupervisors\u0026nbsp;signed a letter\u003c/a\u003e to Gov. Kathy Hochul asking the state to consider adjusting its tax cap formula. The supervisors asked for\u0026nbsp;more flexibility to address \"the growing financial pressures facing local governments.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe letter stressed that municipal budgets are forced to \"absorb significant costs that we have no vote, voice or authority to determine.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSmithtown eliminated more than\u0026nbsp;30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025,\u0026nbsp;Smithtown Comptroller Paul Rubano said.\u0026nbsp;The only way to bring down health insurance and retirement costs is to cull the full-time headcount.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The Town has very few options for controlling this cost other than cutting services by shrinking the workforce,\" Rubano said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn North Hempstead,\u0026nbsp;the town has\u0026nbsp;over the past two years offered voluntary buyout programs to help reduce\u0026nbsp;health insurance costs.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"As positions are refilled, new hires enter at lower base salary tiers and typically contribute a higher percentage toward their health insurance premiums,\" Mignardi said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAddressing rising healthcare costs \"is one of the biggest, if not the biggest\u0026nbsp;challenge facing municipalities,\" said Chris Koetzle, executive director of the New York Association of Towns.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLabor unions have extracted attractive benefits for their workers and amassed powerful followings that have led to surging costs, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I think local governments are doing everything they can,\" Koetzle said. \"They're just stuck.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003cem\u003eNewsday's Denise M. Carmine Macchia and Officer Al Sabia were in pursuit of a stolen vehicle when their unmarked police car collided with a truck at a Lindenhurst intersection.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBoth vehicles flipped over and burst into flames.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe law enforcement officers were rushed to Brunswick Hospital in Amityville where Macchia, 32, died from his injuries. Sabia was injured but survived.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNearly 50 years later, the ultimate sacrifices of Macchia as well as four other officers were made known to all who step inside the First Precinct in West Babylon as Suffolk County officials, family members and the Suffolk County Police Foundation unveiled an Honor Wall in their remembrance on Monday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"When you lose someone you love, it hurts. And that hurt doesn't go away,\" Suffolk County Executive Edward P. Romaine said. \"They say as long as you are remembered, they’re never gone.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnder the words \"Hope,\" \"Courage\" and \"Sacrifice,\" plaques honoring five fallen officers from the precinct lined the wall: Patrolman George A. Frees, Patrolman Frank D. Cataldo, Officer William V. DeRosa, Det.\u0026nbsp;Carmine Macchia and Det.\u0026nbsp;Stephen J. Mullen.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMonday's unveiling was the first of seven ceremonies to take place in Suffolk County police precincts through mid-February.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLisa Tuozzolo VanDenburg, co-founder of the foundation, said she felt compelled to give back\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/paul-tuozzolo-nypd-cop-killed-by-manuel-rosales-in-bronx-officials-say-y52213\"\u003e\u0026nbsp;after her husband, NYPD\u0026nbsp;Sgt. Paul Tuozzolo\u003c/a\u003e, was killed in the line of duty 10 years ago.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Knowing that I have a plaque in the precinct where Paul was, it gives me comfort knowing that every new officer that comes through the department will always be able to look back and see and remember Paul,\" she said. \" And I think for the families here today, it's most important that they see that their loved ones are remembered.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLou Civello, president of the Suffolk County Police Benevolent Association, said it was fitting to honor the fallen at their precinct, otherwise referred to as \"house\" by officers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We do that because this is our home,\" Civello said. \"This is the place we come to bond with our blue family. The place we come for strength and guidance. It's a very difficult job, and having that blue family having this precinct, and having this house, this home is critically important to doing that job.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFamily members gathered in the confines of the precinct’s lobby on Monday morning, as the stories of the fallen were recalled. Bagpipes played \"Amazing Grace\" as the wall was unveiled, a white circular wreath standing next to the plaques.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMargaret Macchia, Det. Macchia's widow,\u0026nbsp;attended the ceremony on Monday with her 10-year-old great-nephew. She told Newsday she hopes people will continue to respect police officers and their sacrifices when looking at the wall.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"They do everything they can for us,\" she said. \"We need them.\" \u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHer late husband was \"there for everybody\" and loved being a police officer. Before working in the Suffolk County Police Department, he served as an NYPD officer for about four years.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDecades later, she said she is grateful how the police community Place's $4M Westbury Avenue project to bring new sidewalks, street repaving","teaserTitle":"Town's $4M revitalization project begins","body":"\u003cp\u003eNorth Hempstead Town began work on the\u0026nbsp;long-awaited\u0026nbsp;reconstruction and beautification of Westbury Avenue in Carle Place on Tuesday morning.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe project will transform the hamlet's main thoroughfare into\u0026nbsp;\"a better heartbeat for the community of Carle Place,\" Supervisor Jennifer DeSena said during an on-site news\u0026nbsp;conference Tuesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe approximately $4 million project will be funded by $2.5 million from Nassau County, which manages the roadway, and\u0026nbsp;$1 million from the\u0026nbsp;federal American Rescue Plan Act. The rest is coming from the town.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe work, to be done by the Hicksville-based contractor Stasi General Contracting, will include sidewalk replacements, street repaving, curb improvements, drainage updates and improved pedestrian crossings for a nearly mile-long stretch of the road from Jamaica Boulevard to Carle Road.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We're rebuilding a road, but that's not the big picture. What we're really building here is a better Westbury Avenue,\" DeSena said. \"We're constructing a safer, more attractive 'Main Street' for the people who live here, work here\u0026nbsp;and visit here.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDeSena added: \"We're making a more welcome environment for the businesses that call Carle Place home.\"\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePlans for the revitalization date back two decades\u0026nbsp;but have long stalled amid bureaucratic challenges, DeSena said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"When you have many layers of government, sometimes they point the finger at each other,\" she said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCouncilman Robert Troiano, who represents Carle Place,\u0026nbsp;said during the news\u0026nbsp;conference that the project would\u0026nbsp;help \"rebuild pride in the Carle Place community for their Westbury Avenue.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"This is a community that takes great pride in its schools ... and its homes,\" Troiano said. \"They are connected, in every way possible. But they've never been quite so proud about their downtown.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLast year, Troiano notified town code enforcement officials of overgrown weeds in the right of way of several storefronts and office buildings on Westbury Avenue.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn an interview,\u0026nbsp;Troiano said\u0026nbsp;the project should be complete\u0026nbsp;by May.\u0026nbsp;A town news release said residents should expect \"occasional lane closures, alternating traffic patterns, temporary detours, and some parking restrictions in the project area.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDominick D'Alonzo, president of the Carle Place Civic Association, told Newsday\u0026nbsp;the \"long overdue\" project would\u0026nbsp;be a boon for the village's small businesses.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It's tough to be a small business in this day and age, and then with COVID, everyone took a hit,\" he said. \"Now, we're starting to get a rebirth.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEric Alexander, director of Vision Long Island, a\u0026nbsp;downtown planning organization, said in an interview the improvements would\u0026nbsp;help walkability in the village,\u0026nbsp;which would\u0026nbsp;help with pedestrian safety and make for a more bustling downtown.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe project represents a\u0026nbsp;\"positive example of pedestrian improvements in communities across Long Island. We need many more,\" he said. He added community members had\u0026nbsp;been pushing for the ability to \"walk into town or park and walk safely, frequent the stores.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe town has undertaken several infrastructure improvements in recent months, including the replacement of the Webster Avenue Bridge and a shoreline stabilization project along Bayview Avenue in Manhasset.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/0292736c-b0f1-4ca6-aee9-38987e8de9b6","title":"AIAudio - educator salaries: 8 of the 10 highest-paid educators in 2025-26 worked in Long Island schools","teaserTitle":"8 of the 10 highest-paid educators in NYS work in LI schools","body":"\u003cp\u003eEight of the 10 highest-paid public school educators in the state worked on Long Island in the 2025-26 school year, with Roslyn’s superintendent topping the list, a Newsday analysis found.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe veteran educator, Allison Brown, received a pay package of $436,975, which included her base salary and unspecified additional pay, according to state data. The second-highest-paid educator was Great Neck schools Superintendent Kenneth Bossert, who earned a total of\u0026nbsp;$420,781.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe 10 highest earners in K-12 schools statewide were all administrators, including nine superintendents and one deputy superintendent. In addition to Bossert, the Great Neck school district had a second administrator in the top 10 — Deputy Superintendent John O'Keefe, with total pay of $375,210.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/a55356d8-7517-417e-89ee-6d7a0a0707eb\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPAY261122_ chart\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFinancial watchdog groups have questioned whether that money should instead be used elsewhere in the school system, and\u0026nbsp;to\u0026nbsp;achieve better academic outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The fact that essentially a bureaucrat and manager is making that type of money is just a negative side effect of bureaucracy,” said Zilvinas Silenas, president of the Empire Center for Public Policy, a conservative-leaning think tank based in Albany.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Why isn't that money put into achieving better results?” he added. “Why isn't this money put into classrooms?”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut supporters have argued competitive compensation packages attract and retain the talent needed to manage schools that will educate the next generation of doctors, electricians and chief executives. They also pointed to the high cost of living on the Island, where homeowners pay among the highest property taxes in the country.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAbout two-thirds of a homeowner's property taxes generally go to fund schools, with payroll\u0026nbsp;the single largest expense for districts.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRobert Lowry, senior education finance and policy analyst at the New York State Council of School Superintendents, said superintendents have a wide range of responsibilities, from high-level decision-making over safety and instruction down to whether the cafeteria has enough healthy food options.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLowry also noted home values are often tied to the quality of the school district.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The question becomes,\u0026nbsp;‘How much is all that worth to you?’ ” he said. “Don't you want to make sure that you have a professional leader of your school system who's up to dealing with all those things?”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eTotal pay on LI nears $6.5 billion\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday's analysis was based on figures obtained from the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System through a Freedom of Information Law request. The annual payroll data covers\u0026nbsp;teachers, administrators, guidance counselors and other staffers who worked in the state’s public schools in 2025-26. It also includes some employees of SUNY colleges. New York City schools\u0026nbsp;employees were excluded from the database.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe combined compensation for more than 264,000 educators across New York topped $20 billion last school year, the state data shows. On the Island,\u0026nbsp;total pay for about\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003e68,000 employees neared $6.5 billion.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/e7babb92-4c11-407c-80aa-fb90ffa1b75d\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPAY261122_html_table\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn the 2025-26 academic year, 79 K-12 and SUNY employees on the Island earned more than $300,000, up from 64 a year prior. Another 1,317 made between $200,000 and $300,000 last school year, up from 1,129 in 2024-25, according to the data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhile SUNY employees were included in the database, Newsday excluded them from the top 10 ranking because\u0026nbsp;salary levels in the statewide university network are not comparable to those set by local school boards.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIsland schools chiefs who appeared on the top earners list also include:\u0026nbsp;Francesco Ianni, of Oyster Bay-East Norwich, who received\u0026nbsp;$412,662;\u0026nbsp;Kathleen Bannon in Copiague, with a $389,246\u0026nbsp;pay package;\u0026nbsp;Kevin Scanlon, of\u0026nbsp;Three Village, with $376,761; Joseph Famularo at Bellmore with $375,771; and Kevin Coster, of William Floyd, with $365,206.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTwo additional administrators — interim Webutuck Central schools Superintendent Raymond Castellani\u0026nbsp;in Dutchess County and Amy Creeden, superintendent of Middletown schools — also were on the list. They made $389,356 and $376,701 respectively.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday reached out to all 10 administrators and their respective school board presidents. They either declined to comment or did not respond to requests for comment. Five districts responded with statements and two noted their superintendents'\u0026nbsp;long tenure as reasons contributing to\u0026nbsp;their pay.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Roslyn, Brown’s base salary for 2025-26 was $363,262. District spokeswoman Cynthia Younker did not say what made up the superintendent’s remaining pay of more than $70,000, but she\u0026nbsp;noted Brown is in her 11th year\u0026nbsp;as superintendent after first joining the district in 2008.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOver nearly two decades in the district, Brown has worked her way up through the ranks, from a principal to an assistant superintendent and later deputy superintendent, according to her biography posted on the district website.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe 3,300-student Nassau district was recently\u0026nbsp;\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/niche-rankings-long-island-school-districts-idkfwe8r\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eranked by Niche as the second-best district\u003c/a\u003e in the country.\u003cspan style=\"background-color: rgba(255, 255, 0, 0.3);\"\u003e \u003c/span\u003eRoslyn High School has consistently \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/regeneron-science-talent-search-long-island-ccm8htc8\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eproduced semifinalists\u003c/a\u003e in the prestigious Regeneron competition and\u0026nbsp;students in the district have won\u0026nbsp;awards ranging from the region’s math fair to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/li-life/roslyn-student-npr-podcast-challenge-yz8zb4h0\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eNPR's Podcast Challenge\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLeonardo Nunez Botto, of Flower Hill, believes Brown’s pay was excessive, especially when compared with other districts: “I think it's quite too much money for the superintendent.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca Botto told Newsday he thinks the Roslyn schools superintendent's salary is excessive.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePat Goldstein, of East Hills, however, said she didn’t have an issue with it as long as the district was willing to pay it. Goldstein’s two adult children graduated from Roslyn schools in 2009 and 2013 and she considered the district to have provided a good education to them.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“I was always satisfied with the programs that they had,” she said. “If they can get it, why not? I'm not going to begrudge them.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Pat Goldstein, meanwhile, was happy with the education her adult children received in the Roslyn school district.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/31cea22f-50b5-4203-9018-7dd6e840d4c7/liPAY261122c.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003ePat Goldstein, meanwhile, was happy with the education her adult children received in the Roslyn school district.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eExperience, academic outcomes cited\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen asked for comment about the superintendent's pay, William Floyd district spokesman\u0026nbsp;James Montalto cited rising graduation rates under Coster’s tenure and his three decades of experience in education.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMontalto also pointed to the district’s size. William Floyd is one of the Island’s biggest districts with 9,500 students, 1,500 staffers and a budget of $332 million.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Since assuming the role in 2015, the district’s graduation rate has increased from 79% to 95%, alongside significant improvements in facilities, an upgrade in the district’s bond rating and expanded educational opportunities in Career and Technical Education, science, music, the arts, athletics, and more,” Montalto wrote in an email.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMontalto said Coster’s base salary for 2025-26 was $325,485 and the additional pay of nearly $40,000 came from a\u0026nbsp;payout for unused sick and vacation time at the end of last school year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWanda Ortiz-Rivera, superintendent of the Island’s largest school district in Brentwood, which serves\u0026nbsp;18,000 students, earned\u0026nbsp;$295,155 last school year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThree Village\u0026nbsp;spokeswoman Denise Nash noted\u0026nbsp;the superintendent's\u0026nbsp;pay figure includes other compensation in addition to\u0026nbsp;Scanlon’s base pay.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThree Village was one of five Island districts that held a revote after residents rejected its initial budget proposal that called for a 4.54% tax levy hike. Voters later approved a lower increase.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnlike the other superintendents whose gross pay went up, Scanlon was the only one on the top earners list whose compensation stayed the same from 2024-25 to 2025-26.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Great Neck, a spokeswoman said the pay figures for Bossert and O'Keefe included\u0026nbsp;base pay and contractual benefits.\u0026nbsp;Bossert and O'Keefe could cash in unused vacation days, and O'Keefe was entitled to an annual “longevity” payment of $6,000, according to their contracts. Both had a car allowance: Bossert at $1,000 per month and O'Keefe at $500.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBossert is also serving as president of the New York State Council of School Superintendents this year.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eGreat Neck schools are \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/education/us-news-world-report-best-schools-nys-htwt8mik\" target=\"_blank\"\u003econsidered among the best\u003c/a\u003e in the state with \u003ca href=\"https://data.nysed.gov/essa.php?instid=800000049062\u0026amp;year=2025\u0026amp;createreport=1\u0026amp;HSgradrate=1\u0026amp;38ELA=1\u0026amp;38MATH=1\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ehigh graduation rates and proficiency levels\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Copiague, a statement from the district said the superintendent's\u0026nbsp;compensation “reflects salary, contractual benefits and payouts for earned but unused sick leave and vacation days in accordance with the terms of Dr. Bannon’s employment agreement.”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBannon has led the district \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/copiague-s-superintendent-to-retire-in-august-and-be-replaced-by-associate-superintendent-x93935\" target=\"_blank\"\u003esince 2015\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBettianne Balzano, who has lived in Copiague for 27 years, said she found Bannon’s total pay to be “ludicrous.”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“It's unfortunate because I think that our taxes are so exorbitant,” she said. “And it's a shame. We live in a beautiful place and I love it here. But a lot of people are being taxed out of here.”\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Bettianne Balzano took issue with the superintendent's compensation.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/dc36fbf4-8d11-488a-acb6-937d2070bc31/DEC_6648.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eBettianne Balzano took issue with the superintendent's compensation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJessica Dejesus, a mother of two, took a different view.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDejesus said she had moved from Brooklyn to Long Island for a better life for her children and she has been pleased with the education her two kids, 9 and 16, received from the Copiague district.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“I really do feel like it is a better life out here,” she said. “The taxes for me personally, I can't speak [for] everyone else, is worth it for my kids to have a better life. Island town and city healthcare premiums climb to $344M, triggering tax hikes","teaserTitle":"'Skyrocket out of control': LI town, city healthcare costs rise to $344M","body":"\u003cp\u003eLong Island towns and cities spent $344.4 million on employee and retiree healthcare premiums last year, a ballooning cost that officials say is expected to trigger\u0026nbsp;tax hikes and further strain municipal budgets.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe total across Long Island's 13 towns and two cities was up about 3% over 2024, and 37% over 2021, according to state data analyzed by Newsday. Municipal officials, facing a Nov. 20 deadline to finalize 2027 spending plans, expect\u0026nbsp;the cost to rise steeply\u0026nbsp;next year.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/9befe63d-b6e5-429f-8e3c-c4e72ce167d9\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: Change in employee, retiree health insurance costs \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOfficials have cited the sharply rising expense of covering employee and retiree\u0026nbsp;healthcare plans as a key driver of annual tax hikes. The benefit can account for more than 15% of some town and city spending plans, making it among their largest single expenses.\u0026nbsp;State-set premiums\u0026nbsp;have risen an average of 6% annually since 2021 and increased\u0026nbsp;nearly 10% in 2026, the highest change in years, state data shows.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHealthcare costs between 2024 and\u0026nbsp;2025\u0026nbsp;rose the most in\u0026nbsp;Long Beach, where the city experienced a 17%, or $2.6 million, jump\u0026nbsp;to $17.6 million. In the Town of Oyster Bay, the expense rose\u0026nbsp;nearly 19%, or $7.1 million, to $45.1 million.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It's unlike almost anything else on our budget,\" Rob Darienzo, Oyster Bay's budget director, said in an interview. \"We do our best to keep our salaries the same, and we try to reduce our debt. And yet, the health insurance premiums, mandated by New York State, they skyrocket out of control.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBudget officials are bracing for \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/town-city-village-pension-spending-tnzljx37\"\u003edouble-digit-percent increases\u003c/a\u003e to healthcare expenses each year,\u0026nbsp;on top of surging employee pension costs. The increases have compelled towns and cities to keep their workforces flat and lean on incentive programs to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/riverhead-employee-retirement-incentive-dla3b8eg\"\u003ereduce the number of highly paid workers\u003c/a\u003e and the cost\u0026nbsp;of their benefits, officials said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNearly 7,000 town and city employees\u0026nbsp;are covered by the New York State Health Insurance Plan. NYSHIP covers about 27,000 dependents on Long Island,\u0026nbsp;according to the\u0026nbsp;state Department of Civil Service, which administers the health plan.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNYSHIP premium rates, which are set by the state, rose\u0026nbsp;2.2% in 2021, 7.4% in 2022, 8.6% in 2023 and 8.9% in 2024 but were flat in 2025, the agency said. Then, in 2026, premium rates jumped\u0026nbsp;9.6%.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/d000832a-cc85-4871-9e2a-caa5cde570c5\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: NYSHIP annual rate increases \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe\u0026nbsp;rate changes are affected by several factors, officials say, from the\u0026nbsp;number of employees enrolled in family plans to\u0026nbsp;increases in\u0026nbsp;the cost of medical procedures.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe rising burden of funding benefit programs\u0026nbsp;is a \"huge problem\" in the long term, said\u0026nbsp;Zilvinas Silenas, president of the\u0026nbsp;Empire Center, a conservative think tank based in Albany.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"If this continues, meaning more and more people claim benefits or the benefits become increasingly generous or even the wages become more generous, there is a finite number of taxpayers in New York that can support that,\"\u0026nbsp;Silenas said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eClimbing costs\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHealthcare costs, along with other annual increases like contractual raises and retirement benefits, make it difficult to stay below the state's 2% tax cap, Southampton Supervisor Maria Moore said. Last year, the town negotiated for\u0026nbsp;new employees to pay 15% of their healthcare benefits, rather than 10%, to help blunt the rising cost\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003eas part of its contract with the Civil Service Employees Association union.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/0e7881d4-7aeb-4576-8252-4b9ddc7a0b9a\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: LI town and city healthcare costs \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"How can you stay below 2% when just the salary increases contractually are 3%, the healthcare is going up 6% more than likely, the pension will likely go up another 10% ... not to mention the cost of gas, diesel [and] materials?\" Moore said. \"Everything costs more now.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSouthampton's healthcare costs\u0026nbsp;have risen from\u0026nbsp;$17 million in 2022 to $22.1 million in 2025, state data shows.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBabylon Deputy Comptroller Cathy Wuertz said governments are in a defensive position\u0026nbsp;while preparing\u0026nbsp;budgets.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We budget conservatively,\" Wuertz said. \"Some years it works in our favor, where we get a couple of bucks that we didn’t have to spend. You budget according to what you think is going to happen, according to trends, and you just go from there.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eFuture concerns\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"North Hempstead Town Hall. The town's healthcare costs are forecast to jump even more next year.\n\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-f=\"3x2\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/dfc3c5ce-3186-441a-9582-311bb1446a83/TOWNHALLS2257782689100506.jpg?f=3x2\u0026amp;w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eNorth Hempstead Town Hall. The town's healthcare costs are forecast to jump even more next year. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe tide of rising healthcare costs isn't expected to recede in the near future, officials said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEast Hampton's 2027 budget anticipated $14.8 million in health insurance costs, a nearly 5% increase over this year.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe state usually releases its official rate increases in late November or December\u0026nbsp;— after town and city budgets are finalized. That means officials\u0026nbsp;base budgets, and project one of their largest expenses,\u0026nbsp;off\u0026nbsp;limited information.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"A lot of that is really just trying to, for lack of a better phrase, sharpening your pencils — looking at prior year history and increases, and really just hoping that you're coming up with as best of an accurate number as possible,\" East Hampton Town Administrator Rebecca Hansen said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOn the national level, healthcare premiums have risen at a fast clip, as more patients sign up for\u0026nbsp;mental health services and undergo\u0026nbsp;expensive treatments,\u0026nbsp;said Matthew Rae, associate director for the healthcare marketplace program at KFF, a Washington, D.C., health policy and research nonprofit. Newer drugs on the market, like GLP-1s and emerging cancer treatments, are also driving premium hikes, Rae said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat leaves employers to shoulder a growing expense.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"What used to be considered an expensive drug was $100,000. There are now a lot of drugs on the market that are $1 million,\" Rae said, referring to treatments for cancers and diseases like sickle cell. \"How we finance that may be a challenge, and for whatever reason we made employers the basis of our healthcare finance system, but we need to figure out how to pay for stuff like that that\u0026nbsp;is remarkably changing people's lives.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn North Hempstead, healthcare costs rose nearly 2% between 2025 and 2026 but\u0026nbsp;are expected to rise almost 6% next year, said Umberto Mignardi, a town spokesman.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCosts have climbed due to \"higher medical facility and physician fees, rising specialty drug and prescription costs, aging active and retiree plan demographics, state-mandated coverage expansions and caps on member out-of-pocket spending,\" Mignardi said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eCreative decisions\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Smithtown Town Hall. The town eliminated more than 30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025. \n\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-f=\"3x2\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/e1a87677-1faf-463d-a8cf-f93fe762b018/TOWNHALLS05914156.jpg?f=3x2\u0026amp;w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eSmithtown Town Hall. The town eliminated more than 30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome towns\u0026nbsp;have resorted to workforce reductions and buyouts to keep pace.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn October, Suffolk County \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/tax-cap-suffolk-supervisors-tavmen4v\"\u003esupervisors\u0026nbsp;signed a letter\u003c/a\u003e to Gov. Kathy Hochul asking the state to consider adjusting its tax cap formula. The supervisors asked for\u0026nbsp;more flexibility to address \"the growing financial pressures facing local governments.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe letter stressed that municipal budgets are forced to \"absorb significant costs that we have no vote, voice or authority to determine.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSmithtown eliminated more than\u0026nbsp;30 part-time seasonal positions in 2025,\u0026nbsp;Smithtown Comptroller Paul Rubano said.\u0026nbsp;The only way to bring down health insurance and retirement costs is to cull the full-time headcount.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The Town has very few options for controlling this cost other than cutting services by shrinking the workforce,\" Rubano said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn North Hempstead,\u0026nbsp;the town has\u0026nbsp;over the past two years offered voluntary buyout programs to help reduce\u0026nbsp;health insurance costs.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"As positions are refilled, new hires enter at lower base salary tiers and typically contribute a higher percentage toward their health insurance premiums,\" Mignardi said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAddressing rising healthcare costs \"is one of the biggest, if not the biggest\u0026nbsp;challenge facing municipalities,\" said Chris Koetzle, executive director of the New York Association of Towns.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLabor unions have extracted attractive benefits for their workers and amassed powerful followings that have led to surging costs, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I think local governments are doing everything they can,\" Koetzle said. \"They're just stuck.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003cem\u003eNewsday's Denise M. Sabia was injured but survived.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNearly 50 years later, the ultimate sacrifices of Macchia as well as four other officers were made known to all who step inside the First Precinct in West Babylon as Suffolk County officials, family members and the Suffolk County Police Foundation unveiled an Honor Wall in their remembrance on Monday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"When you lose someone you love, it hurts. Romaine said. \"They say as long as you are remembered, they’re never gone.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnder the words \"Hope,\" \"Courage\" and \"Sacrifice,\" plaques honoring five fallen officers from the precinct lined the wall: Patrolman George A. Frees, Patrolman Frank D. Cataldo, Officer William V. DeRosa, Det.\u0026nbsp;Carmine Macchia and Det.\u0026nbsp;Stephen J. Mullen.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMonday's unveiling was the first of seven ceremonies to take place in Suffolk County police precincts through mid-February.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLisa Tuozzolo VanDenburg, co-founder of the foundation, said she felt compelled to give back\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/new-york/paul-tuozzolo-nypd-cop-killed-by-manuel-rosales-in-bronx-officials-say-y52213\"\u003e\u0026nbsp;after her husband, NYPD\u0026nbsp;Sgt. Paul Tuozzolo\u003c/a\u003e, was killed in the line of duty 10 years ago.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Knowing that I have a plaque in the precinct where Paul was, it gives me comfort knowing that every new officer that comes through the department will always be able to look back and see and remember Paul,\" she said. \" And I think for the families here today, it's most important that they see that their loved ones are remembered.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLou Civello, president of the Suffolk County Police Benevolent Association, said it was fitting to honor the fallen at their precinct, otherwise referred to as \"house\" by officers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We do that because this is our home,\" Civello said. \"This is the place we come to bond with our blue family. The place we come for strength and guidance. It's a very difficult job, and having that blue family having this precinct, and having this house, this home is critically important to doing that job.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFamily members gathered in the confines of the precinct’s lobby on Monday morning, as the stories of the fallen were recalled. Bagpipes played \"Amazing Grace\" as the wall was unveiled, a white circular wreath standing next to the plaques.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMargaret Macchia, Det. Macchia's widow,\u0026nbsp;attended the ceremony on Monday with her 10-year-old great-nephew. Suffolk County’s Cold Case Task Force, Suffolk District Attorney Ray Tierney said on Thursday, allowed\u0026nbsp;authorities to identify six dead and previously unknown people, including three believed to be homicide victims.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The six individuals in these cases remained nameless for decades, with the oldest case dating back 50 years to 1976,” Tierney said at a news conference in Brentwood. “Through the dedicated work of those partners in the cold case task force, we have made meaningful progress in restoring the identities of these individuals, providing answers to their loved ones and advancing the pursuit of justice on their behalf.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“We’ve given\u0026nbsp;back their names,” Tierney added, “and that’s not insignificant.”\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe technology used to identify the homicide victims, next generation sequencing, was \u0026nbsp;used to identify Gilgo Beach victims Karen Vergata and Valerie Mack, Tierney said. It was also important in the prosecution of admitted Gilgo Beach serial killer Rex A. Heuermann.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk officials also used DNA technology to determine Michelle Chronick Tyson, 59, of Virginia, was responsible for the death of her newborn baby in 1996. She was extradited from Virginia to Suffolk last month and charged with second-degree murder, Tierney said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk’s Cold Case Task Force is a partnership between the district attorney’s Cold Case Unit and the county’s police department, according to officials, who urged anyone with information about the newly identified individuals to \u0026nbsp;call Suffolk Crime Stoppers at 800-220-8477.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“It’s about the victims, about Suffolk County never forgetting those victims, and making sure that they’re identified, and ultimately the people involved face justice,” Suffolk Police Commissioner Kevin Catalina said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eSeveral homicide victims\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe homicide victims include \"Raymond Doe,\" who was found on Nov. 27, 1976, when three hunters discovered the remains of a man who had been severely burned in Deer Park. Investigators determined the cause of death was a gunshot wound to his lower right abdomen. The victim was known as Raymond Doe because of the “Raymond” tattoo on his left arm.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk cold case investigators have identified the man as Ramon Perez y Rivera, a native of Puerto Rico who lived in South Williamsburg, Brooklyn. He was approximately 41 at the time of his death.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOfficials also unveiled who the woman known as \"Montauk Mary\" was.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eShe was\u0026nbsp;found when a U.S. airman on his lunch break discovered the body of an elderly woman near the parking lot of East Overlook Park on Montauk Highway on March 22, 1978. The medical examiner’s office determined the woman had been shot four times and had only been dead for a few hours.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eInvestigators identified the woman as Sofia Margherita Marrone, of Pleasantville, New Jersey. Authorities suspect Marrone may have been a victim of Richard Biegenwald, aka the “Jersey Shore Thrill Killer,” who Tierney said had been linked to numerous\u0026nbsp;homicides between 1958 and 1982. Biegenwald died in 2008.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“While we have not been able to forensically tie Mr. Biegenwald to the crime thus far, the investigation is still going on,” Tierney said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Heckscher Jane Doe\" was found on April 2, 1978, after a man walking his dog along the beach at Heckscher State Park in East Islip discovered what appeared to be a human skull in the sand. Law enforcement later uncovered a set of human\u0026nbsp;remains. A belt was tightly bound around the victim’s neck\u0026nbsp;and an autopsy determined the cause of death was strangulation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAuthorities identified the victim 48 years later as Antoinette Rugg, of Lindenhurst, who was 26 and had a 10-year-old son at the time of her death. The son attended Thursday’s news conference but did not speak to reporters.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Suffolk County District Attorney Raymond A. The cause of death remains under investigation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOfficials have identified the woman as Kyong-Ok Kim, of South Korea. Kim had gotten married and moved to Michigan in 1978.\u0026nbsp;Kim moved to New York around 1985 and resided in Woodside, Queens, at the time of her death. She was 32 years old when she died.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe U.S. Coast Guard found the remains of \"John Doe\" approximately 9 miles south of Fire Island on Nov. 4, 1990. The cause of death is believed to be drowning. Investigators have identified him as Omelios Steward, of Brooklyn, who was 26 at the time of his death. Authorities have identified the man as Andreas Kupke, a German tourist. He arrived at Newark International Airport but never boarded his return flight.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"These developments represent more than just investigative milestones,\" Tierney said. \"They represent a shared principle that no victim should ever be forgotten.\"\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/d924de35-33ef-4516-a56e-668699d4fbe8","title":"AIAudio -
