On LI, it still has sole.","body":"\u003cp\u003eAlessandro \"Alex\" Piscitelli remembers being a 5-year-old watching in amazement as his father stitched worn footwear and other leather goods\u0026nbsp;back to life at his Greenlawn shoe repair shop in 1968.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBy the time Piscitelli\u0026nbsp;graduated\u0026nbsp;high school, he had learned enough of the craft to start working full time at the shop, which was\u0026nbsp;opened in 1954 by his father, Mario Piscitelli, an immigrant from Durazzano, Italy.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I saw the people,\"\u0026nbsp;said Alex Piscitelli, who took over Mario’s Shoe Repair in 1982.\u0026nbsp;\"It was busy in and out, so busy, and I says, ‘You know, I could make a living here.’ \"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMore than four decades later, Piscitelli is part of a small group of Long Island cobblers that has bucked a sharp nationwide decline. Cobblers are shoe repair professionals who also work on belts, handbags, luggage and other leather goods, often using specialized stitching, polishing and restoration techniques.\u0026nbsp; \u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLong Island had 16 footwear and leather-goods repair establishments in 2025, up from 13 in 2005, a 23% increase, according to the latest data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. Over the same 20-year period, the number of establishments fell 42% both nationwide and in New York State, to 663 and 90, respectively. \u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Alessandro Piscitelli repairs a leather belt using a sewing machine at Mario's Shoe Repair in Greenlawn. He learned the trade from his father, who opened the shop in 1954.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/df9dc4c0-0c36-49bd-81b2-1c1b9de99a68\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/df9dc4c0-0c36-49bd-81b2-1c1b9de99a68', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/df9dc4c0-0c36-49bd-81b2-1c1b9de99a68\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/df9dc4c0-0c36-49bd-81b2-1c1b9de99a68/BZCOBBLERS261108-5.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eAlessandro Piscitelli repairs a leather belt using a sewing machine at Mario's Shoe Repair in Greenlawn. He learned the trade from his father, who opened the shop in 1954.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLong Island repair businesses may have an advantage because many are located in or near high-income areas where residents can afford to buy expensive shoes and see value in repairing them, shop owners and industry experts said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut their numbers remain\u0026nbsp;small, and Long Island has lost a few longtime shops in recent years.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Village Cobbler Shoppe in Riverhead closed in 2024, after 53 years in business.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAndrea’s Shoe Repair in Huntington closed this year after the death of the shop’s owner, Andrea Sorrentino, who was a mentor to Piscitelli. Sorrentino, who\u0026nbsp;died in June at age 90,\u0026nbsp;opened his shoe store around 1976, according to a \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/obituaries/andrea-sorrentino-huntington-mu1funo7\"\u003eNewsday obituary\u003c/a\u003e published in June.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSeveral challenges help explain why fewer people are entering the shoe repair\u0026nbsp;trade and why shops continue to disappear, said Mitch Lebovic, administrator of the Shoe Service Institute of America, a trade group based in Wheaton, Illinois. Among them\u0026nbsp;is the\u0026nbsp;lack of succession plans at many mom-and-pop businesses when owners retire or die, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003c/strong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe industry also is contending with changes in how people work and dress. The number of people working in office buildings — and wearing professional attire — has not returned to the levels that existed before the COVID-19 pandemic,\u0026nbsp;Lebovic said.\u0026nbsp;The pandemic\u0026nbsp;started in early\u0026nbsp;2020 and ended in May 2023.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAdding to the\u0026nbsp;business\u0026nbsp;challenges is the growth of fast fashion, which has flooded the market with inexpensive shoes that can cost less to replace than to repair.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Piscitelli uses a sewing machine to stitch a leather belt. Some of the machines he uses in his shop are more than 100 years old.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/5caed318-cc8b-4141-962c-3379e6a9215a\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/5caed318-cc8b-4141-962c-3379e6a9215a', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/5caed318-cc8b-4141-962c-3379e6a9215a\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/5caed318-cc8b-4141-962c-3379e6a9215a/BZCOBBLERS261108-7.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003ePiscitelli uses a sewing machine to stitch a leather belt. Some of the machines he uses in his shop are more than 100 years old.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eClothing and footwear companies are under increasing pressure to produce and sell cheaper goods, making it harder for repair shops to compete with the price of simply buying something new, said sustainability expert Sandra Goldmark, who is a\u0026nbsp;professor of professional practice and associate dean for engagement and impact at the Columbia Climate School.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"If a new shoe costs $20 and it costs $25 to repair it, obviously that’s a really hard case to make\u0026nbsp;—\u0026nbsp;even for someone who wants to keep their shoes,\" she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFurthermore, many of today's shoes are made of cheap materials that make them harder to fix than higher-quality shoes, she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eShoe repair shop owners interviewed by Newsday said those still operating in the region remain busy, even as fewer people enter the trade and longtime businesses\u0026nbsp;continue to disappear nationwide.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhat it takes to keep a shoe repair shop going\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Luis O. Sandoval, a second-generation cobbler, displays a luxury handbag more than 30 years old that he restored at Sandy's Shoe Repair in Syosset. The shop has expanded its luxury-brand restoration services.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/5fabc32a-64c5-4a30-833f-b83b3bab5270\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/5fabc32a-64c5-4a30-833f-b83b3bab5270', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/5fabc32a-64c5-4a30-833f-b83b3bab5270\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/5fabc32a-64c5-4a30-833f-b83b3bab5270/BZCOBBLERS261108_13.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eLuis O. Sandoval, a second-generation cobbler, displays a luxury handbag more than 30 years old that he restored at Sandy's Shoe Repair in Syosset. The shop has expanded its luxury-brand restoration services.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLuis O. Sandoval is a second-generation owner of Sandy’s Shoe Repair in Syosset, which his father, Luis A. Sandoval, founded in the Bronx in the early 1980s under a different name. \u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe younger Sandoval began working in the Bronx shop at age 11, learning the tools of the trade from his father, who had co-owned a shoe manufacturing factory with his brother in Colombia before immigrating to New York in 1978.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The shoe repair industry\u0026nbsp;has always been in my blood,\" said\u0026nbsp;Luis O. Sandoval, 55, adding that he also was drawn to the work because he wanted to spend time with his father.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBy the late 1980s, the elder Sandoval owned five shoe repair\u0026nbsp;shops in the Bronx and one on Long Island, in Farmingdale.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHe relocated with his family —\u0026nbsp;a wife and three children\u0026nbsp;—\u0026nbsp;from the Bronx to Farmingdale in\u0026nbsp;1990, and moved the Farmingdale store to Syosset in\u0026nbsp;1991, his son said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHe had sold all of his shops, except the one in Syosset, by the late 1990s\u0026nbsp;because of the heavy demands of running the locations, his son said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"He found it [to be]\u0026nbsp;too much. He didn't want to have the hassle and the\u0026nbsp;bustle\u0026nbsp;of owning shops and going\u0026nbsp;in there and checking on everything\u0026nbsp;and everyone. He just wanted to concentrate on the one that was the most successful,\u0026nbsp;which was Syosset,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLuis O. Sandoval took over the business after his father died in 2020 at age 74.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSandoval said he initially wanted to forge his own path rather than follow his father into the family business.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I did my college thing. I went on my own,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut after his father died, Sandoval found himself drawn back to the shop.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Little did I know after he passed, I would end up coming in loving the business more than ever,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSandoval said expanding the shop's luxury-brand restoration services in 2020 has helped keep business steady during slower periods.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSandoval said his father also taught him the importance of helping customers understand the value of shoe repairs.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"My father taught me: If you talk to the customer and educate them, their value systems change, and they see the benefit of a shop like mine. And I’ve been able to keep that up,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBeing in Syosset, a high-income area, also helps\u0026nbsp;his business, said Sandoval, who brings on\u0026nbsp;two freelance\u0026nbsp;cobblers when extra hands are\u0026nbsp;needed.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Shoes awaiting repair line shelves at Mario's Shoe Repair, where Piscitelli works alone and handles everything from worn heels to leather restoration.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/a089e568-081e-411f-b7fb-b00d98430920\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/a089e568-081e-411f-b7fb-b00d98430920', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/a089e568-081e-411f-b7fb-b00d98430920\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/a089e568-081e-411f-b7fb-b00d98430920/BZCOBBLERS261108-15.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eShoes awaiting repair line shelves at Mario's Shoe Repair, where Piscitelli works alone and handles everything from worn heels to leather restoration.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNationwide, shoe repair shops that are doing well\u0026nbsp;these days tend to be in or near high-income areas where residents can afford to buy expensive shoes that are worth the cost of repairs, Lebovic said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn 2024, the median household income\u0026nbsp;in Syosset\u0026nbsp;was $187,273 and the poverty rate was 4.2%, while\u0026nbsp;in Greenlawn, the median household income was\u0026nbsp;$164,427 and the poverty rate was 6.3%,\u0026nbsp;according to the latest U.S. Census Bureau data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFor comparison, the median household incomes and poverty rates were $130,686 and 6.7%, respectively, in Suffolk County; $146,202 and 5.9% in Nassau County; $85,974 and 13.8% in New York State; and $80,734\u0026nbsp;and 10.2% in the nation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSmall businesses that repair shoes have to factor in their rising expenses,\u0026nbsp;such as rent and labor,\u0026nbsp;when setting their prices, which can sometimes be high enough to\u0026nbsp;turn off customers, Goldmark said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"A repair person needs to pay themselves a living wage in New York City or Long Island or wherever, and that is competing with wages that are much lower overseas, typically where these shoes are being manufactured,\" she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome successful shoe repair businesses have started mail-in repair operations to be more competitive, Lebovic said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"There’s still people wearing quality shoes. A lot of people don’t know where to send them [for repairs]. So\u0026nbsp;many of today’s cobblers are taking to social media to develop a social media presence, and then from that social media presence, building a mail-in business,\" he\u0026nbsp;said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMany shoe repair shops today lack succession plans because younger generations don’t have an interest in the family businesses, which require on-the-job training because formal footwear repair training programs are\u0026nbsp;difficult to find, he said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"So\u0026nbsp;a lot of people, if they can’t find a family member, if they can’t find an apprentice, they simply close up shop,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSandoval’s 19-year-old daughter, who is a college student majoring in business, might\u0026nbsp;at some point\u0026nbsp;take over his business as an owner who employs people to do the shoe repairs, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"If you have a good quality cobbler in the back, you don’t necessarily need to do the work. You just need to make sure the work is done correctly and properly,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Family photographs and mementos hang at Mario's Shoe Repair, a business passed from father to son. Piscitelli took over the shop in 1982.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/6c9378b4-04fa-41a4-b12c-82b912382f45\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/6c9378b4-04fa-41a4-b12c-82b912382f45', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/6c9378b4-04fa-41a4-b12c-82b912382f45\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/6c9378b4-04fa-41a4-b12c-82b912382f45/BZCOBBLERS261108-12.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eFamily photographs and mementos hang at Mario's Shoe Repair, a business passed from father to son. Piscitelli took over the shop in 1982.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlex Piscitelli plans to keep working as long as he can, but his four adult children won’t be taking over Mario’s Shoe Repair\u0026nbsp;after he retires, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I knew what I wanted to do, but you don’t want to force your kids to do anything. I got successful kids, you know?\"\u0026nbsp;\u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlso\u0026nbsp;he and his wife, Stephanie, want their children to be in careers in which health insurance will be provided by employers, which wouldn’t be the case if they were owners of the repair shop, they said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe couple are insured through Stephanie’s job as a full-time aide at a high school.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhen repairs are worth it\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Mary Beth White, of Huntington Station, picks up her husband's repaired shoes from Piscitelli. Repeat customers and personal service help sustain traditional repair shops.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/e9351476-1845-439f-9c01-3965a8144440\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/e9351476-1845-439f-9c01-3965a8144440', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/e9351476-1845-439f-9c01-3965a8144440\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/e9351476-1845-439f-9c01-3965a8144440/BZCOBBLERS261108-11.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eMary Beth White, of Huntington Station, picks up her husband's repaired shoes from Piscitelli. Repeat customers and personal service help sustain traditional repair shops.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFor\u0026nbsp;Alex Piscitelli, learning the cobbler trade from his father\u0026nbsp;was rewarding, but demanding.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It was tough. ... He was strict with me,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePiscitelli took over Mario’s Shoe Repair in 1982, after his father was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. His father died at age 50 in 1988.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUsing repair machines that are more than 100 years old, Piscitelli is a solo operator who enjoys the craft of giving new life to worn-out shoes. Decades ago, he developed a sixth sense for what stitch would work, what polish would be best and what heel could be smoother, he said. But he also is honest with customers when they should cut their losses and throw away the shoes, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"If they’re going to get worse, what good is it to me to fix the shoes and then I give them back and they break in a week?\" said Piscitelli, 63, adding that unscrupulous practices like that would hurt his reputation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHe’s earned a good living as a cobbler, having bought a home in 1984\u0026nbsp;with his wife and later put his children through college.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Piscitelli, right, talks with Northport customer Richard Propper. Despite a nationwide decline in footwear and leather-goods repair businesses, their number on Long Island rose 23% from 2005 to 2025.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/9c5086b2-d7a0-4ca7-a566-d716876d6cb2\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/9c5086b2-d7a0-4ca7-a566-d716876d6cb2', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/9c5086b2-d7a0-4ca7-a566-d716876d6cb2\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/9c5086b2-d7a0-4ca7-a566-d716876d6cb2/BZCOBBLERS261108-10.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003ePiscitelli, right, talks with Northport customer Richard Propper. Despite a nationwide decline in footwear and leather-goods repair businesses, their number on Long Island rose 23% from 2005 to 2025.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIt helps that he owns the Greenlawn building occupied by the repair shop, so the steep rent challenging other small businesses on Long Island isn’t an issue for him, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn mid-October, Huntington resident Rosalie Paradiso picked up a pair of black, sparkly high heels at Mario’s, which fixed the straps on her \"going-out, party shoes\" for $20.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIt was her first time in Mario’s; her regular repair place, Andrea’s Shoe Repair, closed this year, she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe comfort of the shoes made them worth fixing, she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Well, a lot of people choose to just go to DSW or online and order online. Yes, I can do that, but if I can’t find the right shoe. ... How many times have I ordered shoes and they went back because they’re not comfortable?\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHuntington resident Steven Spucces, a financial adviser, wears \"corporate casual\" clothes to his job in Melville, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn mid-October, he paid $68\u0026nbsp;for scuff-mark removal and polishing for one pair of Ferragamo shoes and two\u0026nbsp;pairs of\u0026nbsp;Cole Haan shoes at Mario’s Shoe Repair, which he visits quarterly for footwear maintenance because he likes the work quality and customer service, said\u0026nbsp;Spucces, 50.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFor him, the repairs are a worthwhile investment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"When you buy expensive, nice shoes, you want to take care of them,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/5511c1e6-85bd-49e9-8808-6b1dfd0edd3e","title":"AIAudio - said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eKleiton De Madeiros, 39, of Montclair, was identified as the man pulled from the water following Wednesday's collapse,\u0026nbsp;authorities said Thursday. Paramedics performed CPR on De Madeiros at the scene and he was taken to a hospital, where he died from his injuries, police said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eA second worker, missing since he fell into\u0026nbsp;Long Creek below the Depression-era\u0026nbsp;bridge, was identified as\u0026nbsp;Diogo De Oliveira, 38, of Elizabeth.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe search for De Oliveira was suspended Thursday afternoon due to high winds and rain, state police said at 3 p.m. It was not immediately clear when the search would resume.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBoth men work for \u003ca href=\"https://www.championssc.com/location/holtsville-regional-office/\"\u003eChampion Painting\u003c/a\u003e, which holds the $13.8 million multilocation bridge contract and has an office in Holtsville.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eState officials said the contract called for workers to repaint and repair steel at four bridges, including the Loop Parkway drawbridge. Officials said the work should be completed by the end of 2027.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Champion is heartbroken for the family of our deceased colleague and closely monitoring the search for our missing team member,\" the company said in a statement. \"We sincerely appreciate the heroism and professionalism of the first responders and thank them for their selfless service. We are focused on the needs of our employees and their families and assisting local, state and federal authorities as they work to determine the cause of this tragic incident.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDe Oliveira’s sister walked down to the beach next to the bridge Thursday morning, joined by friends and family from New Jersey. \n\u003cp\u003eEight workers were doing construction on the drawbridge when the scaffolding collapsed around 11:50 a.m. Wednesday and two fell into the water, state police said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe six other workers did not fall into the water and\u0026nbsp;sustained non-life-threatening injuries, authorities said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOn Thursday morning authorities canvassed the waters of Jones Bay and both sides of the bridge in the search for De Oliveira. \u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eA Nassau County police helicopter circled overhead while police boats from state and Nassau police searched both sides of the bridge, along with the U.S. Coast Guard and Bay Constable.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMeanwhile, state police were stationed at the top of the clinical laboratory sciences, public health, microbiology\u0026nbsp;and biomedical sciences.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eU.S. Merchant Marine Academy ($453,000)\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/united-states-merchant-marine-academy-c72480\"\u003eThe service academy\u003c/a\u003e has programs in marine engineering, marine engineering systems, marine transportation\u0026nbsp;and other related areas of study.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eColumbia University ($364,000)\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/columbia-university-in-the-city-of-new-york-a90146\"\u003eIvy League university’s\u003c/a\u003e academic offerings span fields\u0026nbsp;including computer science, economics, political science, psychology\u0026nbsp;and history.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch1\u003eNY colleges with lowest ROIs\u003c/h1\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eArts colleges account for many of the lowest-ranked schools in New York State’s 10-year ROI rankings, producing negative estimated returns, meaning the earnings associated with these programs are less than what it costs to attend them. Jeff Strohl, director of Georgetown's Center on Education and the Workforce,\u0026nbsp;said that the ROI data does not reflect the personal rewards arts school students gain from getting the education that they want. \"There is a self-fulfillment aspect that isn’t, can’t be monetized,\" he said. \"So the question that we need to ask is, to the art major, 'Are you happy?'\u0026nbsp;\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThose with the lowest ROIs\u0026nbsp;were:\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/464ca1bf-56fc-4a43-bdaa-86fcd117c236\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/464ca1bf-56fc-4a43-bdaa-86fcd117c236', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/464ca1bf-56fc-4a43-bdaa-86fcd117c236\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: NYSCOLLROI-worst\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eManhattan School of Music (-$134,000)\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/manhattan-school-of-music-v37800\"\u003eThe school offers bachelor's degrees for music, jazz arts\u0026nbsp;and musical theater majors\u003c/a\u003e.\u0026nbsp;\"Careers in the performing and visual arts often follow very different trajectories from more conventional professions,\" Jeff Breithaupt, the school's vice president, said in a statement. Alumni hold Pulitzer Prizes, as well as Emmy, Tony and Grammy awards, and have had \"careers on the world's greatest stages,\" among other accomplishments that \"cannot be measured within the first 10 years after enrollment.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eSchool of Visual Arts (-$92,000)\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/school-of-visual-arts-i94873\"\u003eThis college — which became a nonprofit last year — focuses on creative and media-related fields\u003c/a\u003e, including design, film, photography and video, and animation. School president\u0026nbsp;Christopher Cyphers said the value of a degree goes beyond what a dataset can capture.\u0026nbsp;\"Measuring the impact of an artist by the income they earn rather than by their crucial contributions,\"\u0026nbsp;Cyphers said in a statement,\u0026nbsp;\"only reinforces society’s notion that their work is unimportant.\" Art and design program graduates \"enter a galaxy of creative industries and establish lasting careers plying their trade.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eThe Julliard School (-$51,000)\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/the-juilliard-school-f60542\"\u003eJulliard's academic programs focus on dance, drama and music\u003c/a\u003e. \"Our graduates go on to build careers as artists, educators, and cultural practitioners, often pursuing advanced degrees and developing portfolio careers,\" Juilliard said in a statement. Such careers \"can take time to develop, with professional opportunities and earnings often growing significantly beyond the first decade after a bachelor’s degree.\" About 40% of current students attend tuition-free, and 95% receive some form of financial aid, the statement continued, which has limited reliance on student borrowing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003ch1\u003eHow to think about college ROI\u003c/h1\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe rankings also highlight a trade-off between lower upfront costs and longer-term earnings. While many SUNY and CUNY campuses post stronger initial ROI because of their lower costs, some private colleges offset higher prices with substantially higher graduate earnings.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFor example, 10 years after enrollment, SUNY’s flagship campuses at \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/stony-brook-university-h13763\"\u003eStony Brook University\u003c/a\u003e and the \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/university-at-buffalo-x17337\"\u003eUniversity at Buffalo\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;both post higher median ROIs than \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/college-guide/new-york/new-york-university-r85061\"\u003eNew York University\u003c/a\u003e — by roughly $44,000 and $9,000, respectively. The data shows NYU's\u0026nbsp;graduates eventually surpass both SBU and UB in ROI after 15 years, reflecting the private university’s higher long-term earnings despite its greater cost.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStrohl said while SUNY and CUNY colleges tend to be regionally oriented, with graduates who stay and work in the same area, other universities may feed more into the national labor market, where there tends to be a greater swing in salaries.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStrohl also warned students against simply looking at all of the \"overwhelming amount\" of ROI data when deciding which institution to attend. He said the data is most useful to students who already have a list of colleges in which they are interested.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"A student needs to look at that information and use it to help guide them on tiebreaks,\" he said, \"help them narrow down their choices a little bit.\"\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/2eed6507-8ef7-428c-a9f8-4e400b130d70\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/2eed6507-8ef7-428c-a9f8-4e400b130d70', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/2eed6507-8ef7-428c-a9f8-4e400b130d70\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: NYSCOLLEGE-relateds\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/f8a22ecc-c27b-4a2f-bbdd-10aa5c218434","title":"AIAudio - Does college pay off in NY? The papers are believed to contain details on hundreds of cases and how, advocates contend, church leaders covered them up.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe diocese told Newsday it has done its part and that nearly two years ago, it handed over thousands of pages to a trust set up for the abuse victims. The documents were then supposed to be transferred to a college or university archive and made accessible to the public. That has not happened.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe head of the trust, Alan Halperin, a Manhattan-based attorney, did not respond to multiple emails and phone messages from Newsday seeking comment. Halperin was selected as trustee by attorneys for the survivors.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Richard Tollner, a survivor, protests outside St. Anthony's High School in South Huntington in 2019.\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/d2b56e1a-cdd2-4981-a798-469e329b237c\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/d2b56e1a-cdd2-4981-a798-469e329b237c', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/d2b56e1a-cdd2-4981-a798-469e329b237c\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/d2b56e1a-cdd2-4981-a798-469e329b237c/LIBISHOP00172744.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eRichard Tollner, a survivor, protests outside St. Anthony's High School in South Huntington in 2019.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAdvocates said the documents need to be released now, something the Archdiocese of New York and other dioceses around the country are doing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Transparency delayed with no explanation is transparency denied,\" said Terry McKiernan, co-director of \u003ca href=\"https://www.bishop-accountability.org/\"\u003eBishop-Accountability.org\u003c/a\u003e, an online database of Catholic clergy sex abuse. \"Survivors have already waited years for the bankruptcies to be settled, and some have died in the meantime. Now they're waiting for the files of their perpetrators to be released.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe documents may provide extensive new information about the sex abuse scandal that shook one of the 10 largest Roman Catholic dioceses in the nation, with 1.2 million baptized Catholics, advocates said. The release also would be significant because in the past, Rockville Centre served as a model for other dioceses seeking to cover up the abuse, McKiernan said — something the church on Long Island has denied.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It would be fabulous to have\" the documents, McKiernan said. \"It is kind of shocking\" that some dioceses around the country are releasing the information.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003e2024 settlement\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe December 2024 settlement came after four years of negotiations. The Diocese of Rockville Centre had declared bankruptcy in October 2020 as it faced hundreds of lawsuits from people who said they were sexually abused by priests when they were minors.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Part of the Rockville Centre settlement agreement is the release of its documents,\" the Rev. Eric Fasano, a spokesman for the diocese, wrote in an email to Newsday. \"The Diocese complied with its obligation to provide those documents to the Trust established for survivors almost two years ago.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHe said the number of pages in the files could total \"in the thousands, if not tens of thousands of pages.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe files could provide far more information than a landmark 2003 Suffolk County \u003ca href=\"https://www.bishop-accountability.org/reports/2003_02_10_SuffolkGrandJury/\"\u003egrand jury report\u003c/a\u003e on abuse in the diocese, McKiernan said. At a minimum, the internal papers also would include cases in Nassau County.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMany survivors have been waiting for years or decades for the confidential documents to be released, said Richard Tollner, who said he has waited for his allegations to be verified since he was abused by a priest as a high school student in the 1970s.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Now the truth can be seen and heard,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe settlement calls for the diocese and the trust to agree on the institution of higher learning at which the papers would be archived. The archive must \"be made available upon request in accordance with the protocols of that institution,\" the settlement states.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFasano said the diocese had not been contacted about which institution might serve as an archive, adding that he did not know why the process had been delayed.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eArchiving the documents\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJames Stang, a Los Angeles-based attorney who represented victims in the bankruptcy proceedings, said the settlement appeared to call for the papers to be archived at a college or university within two years of the settlement. That would mean by December.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe settlement also states \"the Trust shall provide such documents relating to any perpetrator for which any claim is sustained by the Trust or a cleric that is on the Credibly Accused List, in redacted form to protect survivors and personal health information.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe prospective release of the documents on Long Island would be similar to part of an agreement reached Oct. 23 by the Archdiocese of New York in an \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/religion/archdiocese-of-new-york-diocese-of-rockville-centre-clergy-sex-abuse-settlement-jbntgp5r\"\u003e$800 million settlement\u003c/a\u003e with 1,300 clergy sex abuse victims, said Jeff Anderson, one of the lead attorneys for victims in both the Long Island and New York settlements.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"St. Patrick's Cathedral in Manhattan is the seat of the Archdiocese of New York.\n\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-f=\"3x2\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/fe2ca456-9a63-4a17-abb7-cf9aec0e0996\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/fe2ca456-9a63-4a17-abb7-cf9aec0e0996', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/fe2ca456-9a63-4a17-abb7-cf9aec0e0996\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/fe2ca456-9a63-4a17-abb7-cf9aec0e0996/crp56951321175.jpg?f=3x2\u0026amp;w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eSt. Patrick's Cathedral in Manhattan is the seat of the Archdiocese of New York. \u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn the Archdiocese of New York case, the files will be archived at Iona University in New Rochelle, according to The New York Times. A spokesperson for Iona, a Catholic institution, denied that, saying, \"Iona is not a party to the settlement and is not taking any documents.\" A spokesperson for the Archdiocese of New York said the location was still being finalized, though it could be \"possibly Iona University, or a similar institution.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMcKiernan said he is not sure what is causing the delay in the Rockville Centre case, though it could be because of difficulties finding a university library willing to take on the task. He said his group had offered to do so and already houses the nation’s largest online and brick-and-mortar collections of Catholic Church abuse scandal documents. Scholars, journalists, attorneys general and others use it, he said. The Bishop-Accountability.org archive is in Waltham, Massachusetts.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut the organization never heard back regarding its offer, McKiernan said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAdvocates prefer that the archives be established at neutral, non-Catholic institutions, he said, but housing the documents at a Catholic college is still better than not releasing them at all.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eLong-sought documents\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIf made public, Rockville Centre’s files would be part of a growing trend to release long-sought internal church documents that shed light on the extent of the abuse and how the church handled it, McKiernan said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Archdiocese of Santa Fe in New Mexico, for instance, gave its archive of clergy sex abuse files to the University of New Mexico, where it is publicly available, McKiernan said. The Archdiocese of New Orleans, as part of its bankruptcy settlement with clergy sex abuse victims, has agreed to provide its archive to Louisiana State University.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe archive in New Mexico contains previously sealed clergy personnel files, victim files, investigative files along with transcripts, depositions, clergy risk assessments and other internal church documents. It contains about 100,000 pages concerning an archdiocese that has about one-quarter the number of baptized Catholics as Rockville Centre does, McKiernan said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Rockville Centre files could \"broaden a new transparency movement,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAnderson, the victims’ attorney, said he wanted to see what files Rockville Centre provided before declaring it sufficient.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"What they are supposed to do and what they do oftentimes are two different things,\" Anderson told Newsday. While Rockville Centre should release large amounts of files, \"I won’t believe it until I see it.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"That is part of what needed to happen,\" he added. \"That is part of the deal that did get made.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe diocese \"has complied with its obligations and has been fully transparent, having already turned over its files to the trust that represents the survivors,\" said Fasano, the diocese spokesman.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUsing bankruptcy, \"Rockville Centre was the first diocese in New York State to have resolved its abuse claims on behalf of survivors nearly two years ago and emerged from the process to continue the ministry of the Church on Long Island,\" Fasano said\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTollner, who was a leader of the victims during the Rockville Centre bankruptcy proceedings, said he and others may finally feel some vindication after years of fighting the church — if all the information comes out.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe documents \"will allow victims to feel that the complaints and claims are verifiable and that their voices can now be heard,\" he said. \"And the proof can now be seen.\"\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/52d452ca-ef69-46f8-9e00-48c046b64bfa","title":"AIAudio - end","body":"\u003cp\u003eThe U.S. Department of Justice and Suffolk County\u0026nbsp;are seeking to end a 40-year-old consent decree related to hiring practices that\u0026nbsp;resulted\u0026nbsp;in a police force with too few people of color and women.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe consent decree has been in place since 1986, following a 1983 lawsuit against Suffolk County filed by the federal government that alleged \"Suffolk County was engaged in a pattern or practice of employment discrimination against women, Blacks and Hispanics with respect to job opportunities in the Suffolk County Police Department.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk denied those allegations at the time, while acknowledging the police department had a \"substantial disproportion\" of women and Black and Hispanic people on the force.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk Police Commissioner Kevin Catalina did not respond\u0026nbsp;to a request for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe decree called for Suffolk to implement procedures to give women and Black and Hispanic people an equal opportunity for employment in the police department as white people, as well as requiring regular reports documenting its efforts. The decree stopped short of setting targets for the number of women or Black or Hispanic officers hired by the department.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFormer Suffolk police officers who were involved in recruitment said the consent decree has had little impact on SCPD’s hiring of minority officers, particularly Black officers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It’s like a dog with no teeth,\" said Damon Barney, a retired SCPD officer who worked in recruitment. \"If you’re not doing anything to enforce it, why bother getting rid of it anyway? What is the motivation of getting rid of something you’re not bothering to enforce?\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOf the 2,681 sworn SCPD officers, just 70 were Black, or 2.6%, according to the most recent numbers from the state Division of Criminal Justice Services. Suffolk County’s population is 7% Black, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHispanics are 13.7% of SCPD and women are 13.2%, compared with 24% and 50% of the county’s population, respectively.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I’m a little disappointed in that nothing has changed over these years and any renewed efforts would have to start from scratch again,\" said Kenneth Williams, a retired SCPD officer who was head of recruitment in the 1990s.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe motion filed Monday says Suffolk County has \"complied with the decree in all material respects\" and asks the court to dissolve the decree.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe attorney representing the Suffolk County police union didn't respond to a request for comment. The union was also a party to the consent decree.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The problems they found in 1986 are\u0026nbsp;still afoot in that county, except the government has changed and the attitudes about these kinds of cases has changed,\" said Randolph McLaughlin, a civil rights attorney and professor of law at Pace University.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Department of Justice declined to comment on this story,\u0026nbsp;but the department recently has been undoing past litigation and action taken by the federal government against police departments. In May 2025, \u003ca href=\"https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-department-justices-civil-rights-division-dismisses-biden-era-police-investigations-and\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ethe Justice Department announced\u003c/a\u003e it was dismissing lawsuits, closing investigations or reversing findings against at least nine local police departments across the country.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"This Department of Justice\u0026nbsp;has turned its back on the civil rights of various communities to be free from improper police practices and hiring,\" McLaughlin said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/investigations/police-diversity-minorities-uy1uks6y\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eNewsday reported\u003c/a\u003e earlier this year that police departments on Long Island had made gains in recent years in hiring Hispanic and women officers. Data from the state shows between 2020 and 2025, the number of Hispanic officers on Long Island police forces increased 31% and the number of female officers was up 15%. The number of Black officers working on Long Island only increased 1% in that time.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk County Police Department also increased the number of minority officers on the force between 2020 and 2025, according to \u003ca href=\"https://criminaljustice.ny.gov/law-enforcement-personnel\" target=\"_blank\"\u003estate data\u003c/a\u003e. The number of Hispanic officers increased by 44%; the number of female officers increased by 24%; and the number of Black officers increased by 9%. The entire department grew by 11% during that time. Despite those increases, the number of minority officers is still not proportionate to the population of the county.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEarlier this year, Catalina told Newsday the goal is to be \"representative of the population we serve,\" and he acknowledged they're not.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I expect to do a lot better,\" he said at the time.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHowever, the proportion of Black officers employed by Suffolk County has hardly changed in a quarter of a century, according to state data. In 2000, SCPD employed 64 Black officers, or 2.4% of the force. In 2025, the department employed 70 Black officers, or 2.6% of the force.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://paper.newsday.com/shortcode/NEW150/edition/0035c5d3-cc96-441e-a2da-d4a04ca5063a?page=ec84b4e3-9a94-4202-8d12-13acf4d69dbc\u0026amp;\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eA Newsday investigation\u003c/a\u003e published in 2021 found Black candidates for policing jobs on Long Island were rejected at a rate three times higher than white candidates and Hispanic candidates were rejected twice as often. In the four years after the 2015 hiring exam, SCPD only hired 16 Black cops out of 1,419 applicants, that investigation found.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWilliams, the former head of recruitment at SCPD, said\u0026nbsp;nothing in the consent decree forced the county to actually hire more minority officers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Nothing would ever come from that,\" Williams said of the decree.\u0026nbsp;\"There were no quotas,\u0026nbsp;even no milestones they had to meet, no targets. Although the MTA will look to raise the amount of fare and toll revenue it brings in by about 4%, the cost to ride the Long Island Rail Road or a New York City bus or subway, or to drive across a bridge or tunnel, could climb by more than that.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLieber said the MTA will make a formal rate increase proposal some time over the next two months, after which public hearings would be held and a fare hike plan would be voted on by the MTA board. If approved, the MTA would hike fares and tolls in back-to-back years. Following its usual schedule of raising rates every other year, the MTA was due for an adjustment in 2025, but delayed implementation until January.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We need to be responsible. The whole point of this was a consistent and predictable, small increase, rather than what happened before, which is wait until the MTA is in the toilet financially and in crisis and then jack it up 10-plus percent,\" Lieber said at the MTA’s monthly Manhattan board meeting Wednesday. \"But do not mistake this for, like, solving the MTA’s budget crisis.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat crisis, MTA officials said, is being driven by runaway costs in several areas, including its door-to-door paratransit services for people with disabilities, healthcare benefits for employees and higher-than-expected wages for workers driven by the contract reached with five LIRR unions after they went on strike in May.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLieber said the MTA wants to work with unions to find efficiencies, including by addressing the \"abuse of vacation and sick time leave\" by some employees. MTA chief financial officer Jai Patel noted that of the 261 work days on the calendar, the MTA expects employees to be available for about 227 — taking about 34 days off each year. But the average MTA employee works 201 days a year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAbout 9% of bus operators, Patel said, take more than 50 days off a year. Although many of those days are unpaid, the bus drivers will often work an extra overtime shift during the week \"and they’re basically whole again,\" Patel said. Meanwhile, the MTA must backfill worker absences using overtime, or cancel bus runs altogether. The MTA has canceled 118,000 bus trips so far in 2026 because there was no driver available, officials said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We've got a substantial percentage of our workforce that shows up less than 160 days a year,\" said Lieber, who wants to streamline disciplinary procedures to more easily fire workers who abuse sick days. \"It's really hard to get those people out the door.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJohn Samuelsen, international president of the Transport Workers Union — the union representing MTA bus operators — expressed skepticism over the agency's numbers, and noted that the increase in workers taking time off coincides with a rise in assaults against bus drivers, who have not been given adequate protection.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRather than looking to harsher penalties for workers, Samuelsen said the MTA should provide incentives for them to come to work, including bonuses for employees who don't use paid sick time.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The amount of stress that this environment puts on transit workers leads to more time off work,\" Samuelsen said in an interview Wednesday. \"So if the MTA is so deluded that they believe that pursuing a system where they can discipline even more transit workers is going to lead to better employee availability, then they haven't learned a thing over the years.\"\u003c/p\u003e","publishedDate":"2026-11-18T22:17:29.181Z","updatedDate":"2026-11-19T01:46:21.795Z","url":"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/transportation/mta-fare-increase-budget-deficit-c1zmtfed","headline":"MTA projects future $1B budget deficit, eyes fare increase next spring","teaserTitle":"MTA projects future $1B budget deficit, eyes fare increase next spring","newsLabel":"none","newsLabel2":"none","subType":"article","disableDeepLink":false,"moveAd":false,"textAudio":{"id":"contentid/dab060d2-f4af-4a69-b88b-0818f6337abf","title":"AIAudio - nearly $300 million deficit next year, with\u0026nbsp;higher-than-anticipated raises won by LIRR union workers following their three-day strike in May projected to cost the agency an additional $180 million per year\u0026nbsp;systemwide, officials said Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat operating shortfall could grow to almost $900 million by 2030,\u0026nbsp;according to MTA officials, who noted there’s little they can do to increase revenue\u0026nbsp;beyond raising fares and tolls.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s monthly board meeting in Manhattan on Wednesday, chief financial officer Jai Patel revealed that\u0026nbsp;after four years of balanced budgets, the transit agency is now anticipating a $297 million deficit in 2027. By 2030, the deficit would grow to $897 million — about $800 million more than the MTA’s last forecast in November. The agency's budget is expected to reach $22.8 billion next year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePatel said the rising deficits are being driven primarily by soaring \"uncontrollable costs,\" including fuel and employee benefits, as well as by wage increases included in contracts recently finalized with five Long Island Rail Road labor organizations and expected to be paid to other MTA workers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe MTA had sought a three-year contract with raises of 3% in each of the first two years and 3.5% in the third, as had already been accepted by most other MTA unions. But the LIRR unions sought a fourth year at 4.5%. \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/transportation/lirr-strike-winners-agmofjao\"\u003eAfter a the strike in May\u003c/a\u003e, the MTA agreed to the raises, and now expects to offer similar raises to other unions in the first year of their next contracts. Because of some concessions, the MTA has said the raise would equal about 3.8%.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePatel said the raises will cost the MTA an extra $180 million per year\u0026nbsp;systemwide, including for New York City subway and bus workers. \"Productivity increases\" would\u0026nbsp;help offset some of the higher-than-projected wages, Patel said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eGilman Lang, general chairman of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen Local 269, which represents LIRR train operators, rejected the suggestion that the new contracts\u0026nbsp;are contributing to the MTA’s financial woes. He noted MTA leaders, and Gov. Kathy Hochul — after suggesting during negotiations that giving in to the unions’ demands would result in steep fare hikes — have both since said the new agreement could be afforded without any impact to riders.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"They repeatedly use this labor force as their scapegoat,\" Lang said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eOther factors include health costs, disability services\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMTA chairman and CEO Janno Lieber said the impact of the added wages is minimal when compared with other soaring costs that are out of the agency's control. As one example, Patel noted health benefit costs for employees are expected to reach $2.7 billion by 2030 — more than double what they were in 2019. Costs for the MTA’s Access-a-Ride transportation service for people with disabilities are similarly projected to rise by 135% over those 11 years.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhile MTA fare and toll revenue increases by about 2% a year, Lieber said other costs, like healthcare and fuel, are climbing 10% annually or more.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTotal labor costs account for about 60% of the MTA’s operating budget. Without productivity increases or other changes to offset rising labor expenses, Patel said closing future deficits \"would require additional action.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe MTA has already achieved $500 million in recurring annual cost cutting since 2023, and has plans for another $250 million in efficiencies by 2029, Patel said.\u0026nbsp;But, \"you cannot cut your way to fiscal stability,\" said MTA Board member Neal Zuckerman, who chairs the board's finance committee.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We can do some of the load, but we cannot do all of it,\" said Zuckerman, who noted the MTA has few tools to improve its finances, \"unless we decide to drive fares up dramatically,\" which he did not expect to do.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We’re not going to do that, but it’s the only real lever we have,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLieber said the MTA will introduce potential solutions for closing next year’s projected deficit when it releases its proposed 2027 budget in November. Adhering to a schedule followed for more than a decade, that plan would include a 4% fare and toll increase next year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eLarger fare hike?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAsked by Newsday if the MTA would consider a larger-than-usual rate hike, Lieber offered no direct answer, but said \"riders should not have to bear\u0026nbsp;the full brunt\" of the rising costs.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"But we need a strategy ... to deal with the reality that we have to balance between the real cost growth and our revenue situation,\" Lieber said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn a statement, Hochul spokesman Sean Butler said:\u0026nbsp;\"The Governor has put riders first since day one, rescuing the MTA from its post-pandemic fiscal cliff while preserving affordability and securing substantial savings. She will continue to push for these priorities.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDespite costs outpacing revenue, Patel said the MTA remains on \"strong financial footing,\" pointing to several encouraging metrics, including booming ridership on the LIRR, which recently became the first MTA agency to post monthly ridership figures higher than pre-COVID levels.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAfter seeing revenues crater during the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused ridership to plummet, the MTA expects to close out 2026 with a balanced budget for the fourth straight year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhile the MTA’s \"finances have stabilized,\" State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, in a statement, said \"the road ahead depends on it successfully executing and communicating strategies to bring riders back and generate savings through greater efficiencies.\"\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/e902c1f0-4add-477a-b9d9-6bc4df9bff3a","title":"AIAudio - The average LIRR employee made $32,988 in overtime last year — behind only MTA Bridges \u0026amp; Tunnels workers, who made $53,626 in OT on average.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAverage total pay for LIRR employees in 2025 was $127,808, according to the report. About half of those workers are in line to get raises totaling about\u0026nbsp;15% over four years under a new contract settlement that ended a three-day LIRR union strike last month.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMTA officials have blamed high overtime, in part, to restrictive work rules that allow workers to pile up overtime hours. Representatives from Edwin's union, the\u0026nbsp;Bridge and\u0026nbsp;Tunnel Officers Benevolent Association, did not respond to a request for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOverall, the MTA spent $1.46 billion in overtime in 2025, according to the Empire Center — about 8% more than in 2024 and the highest ever for the transit authority in a single year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe overtime bill represented about 17% of all compensation for the MTA’s 62,000 employees.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHigh overtime costs have been a\u0026nbsp;persistent issue at the MTA for years, leading in 2019 to multiple investigations, indictments and the eventual conviction of five workers on fraud charges for lying about overtime they didn't earn. That year, the MTA adopted several reforms aimed at\u0026nbsp;reducing\u0026nbsp;overtime costs, including biometric time clocks that required employees to scan their fingers at the beginning and end of their work day.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAfter the MTA temporarily suspended the finger-scanning requirement amid sanitary concerns during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and replaced it with an ID card scanning requirement, some LIRR workers began using counterfeit ID cards to scan each other into and out of work, according to an MTA inspector general's investigation last year. The MTA reinstated the finger-scanning requirement in September 2024.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt a state budget hearing in February, MTA Chairman Janno Lieber defended the transit authority's overtime spending, which he noted had fallen as a percentage of the MTA's overall budget in recent years. He said increases\u0026nbsp;in total overtime are, in part, attributable to contractual wage increases.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLieber also drew a distinction between \"good overtime and bad overtime,\" with the former being used to carry out infrastructure work outside of rush hours.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMTA budget documents attributed the higher-than-expected overtime \n\u003cp\u003eCounty officials\u0026nbsp;agreed to pay $100,000 to the EPA, court records show, and adhere to a number of deadlines to shut down the cesspools lining Nassau's North Shore. A cesspool beneath the Bailey Arboretum in Locust Valley, for instance, must be inoperable by July 2028. At least one cesspool located at the Muttontown Preserve was set to close this week, records show.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIf Nassau does not abide by its deadlines and reporting mandates, it faces penalties of up to $750 per violation per day. After 60 days of non-compliance, those penalties jump to $2,000 per day.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We’ve reached an agreement that will deliver on environmental protections for Nassau County residents,\" EPA Regional Administrator Michael Martucci wrote in a statement to Newsday. He added that\u0026nbsp;the agency looked forward to\u0026nbsp;\"continuing our close relationship with the County as they close these cesspools to prevent the spread of contamination.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn a statement to Newsday, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman wrote that the county \"continues to work with our partners at the EPA to update septic systems at our acquired properties. These updates are an environmental victory for Nassau County that improves our infrastructure and benefits the health and safety of our taxpayers.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe EPA's legal filing and settlement followed a yearslong effort by the federal agency and predating Blakeman's tenure\u0026nbsp;to decommission\u0026nbsp;Nassau's large cesspools.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFive of the cesspools named by the government are located in the Muttontown Preserve, with two beneath Nassau Hall and two under Chelsea Mansion. The small Village of Muttontown is among Long Island’s wealthiest enclaves, with the median household income reaching nearly a quarter-million dollars, \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/real-estate/muttontown-vhwrqngh\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eNewsday has reported\u003c/a\u003e. The village mayor could not immediately be reached.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFour other cesspools named in the lawsuit are located in the Sands Point Preserve, with one at the children’s learning center and another at the historic Hempstead House. Nassau lawmakers representing the Sands Point and Muttontown Preserves could not immediately be reached Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026nbsp;Among many environmental issues ranging from flooding roads to storm damage, residents say contaminated drinking water poses the greatest risk to Long Island over the next 10 years, according to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/environment/poll-finds-w2f1ff6o\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ea recent Newsday/Siena poll\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Suffolk, officials have been \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/environment/suffolk-replacement-mandates-ijlujz5z\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eworking for years\u003c/a\u003e to replace every polluting septic tank and cesspool across the county.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAdrienne Esposito, executive director of the Citizens Campaign for the Environment, said Wednesday that\u0026nbsp;the situation in Nassau was \"terrible,\" noting \"100% of Long Island’s drinking water comes from underground.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Every septic and cesspool is leaching into our drinking water system and drains into the marine environment. chemicals' in drinking water: 7 Long Island districts above federal limits, working on treatment","teaserTitle":"7 LI water districts have 'forever chemicals' above federal limits, analysis finds","body":"\u003cp\u003eA year after the Biden administration set\u0026nbsp;strict drinking water limits for \u0026quot;forever chemicals,\u0026quot;\u0026nbsp;seven of the 36 Long Island districts that have submitted data reported annual averages that exceeded the limit,\u0026nbsp;according to a Newsday analysis.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWater suppliers, many of which are installing treatment systems,\u0026nbsp;have until 2029 to comply with the \u003ca href=\"https://www.epa.gov/pfas\"\u003eEnvironmental Protection Agency’s new rule\u003c/a\u003e about the six chemicals, so these results don’t yet amount to a violation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut the drinking water standards\u0026nbsp;are being challenged in a lawsuit filed by chemical manufacturers and water providers, which\u0026nbsp;could render that deadline irrelevant.\u0026nbsp;The Trump administration is weighing whether to defend the limits, and must respond to the lawsuit by Monday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIf the federal standards are overturned, New York’s own drinking water standard would remain in effect, but the state limit is less strict and applies to just two PFAS compounds, not six.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat could\u0026nbsp;leave Long Islanders' and other New Yorkers' drinking water with PFAS contamination levels that federal regulators and\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003ehealth experts say are not safe\u003cstrong\u003e,\u003c/strong\u003e the federal data shows.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWithout federal limits, some Long Island communities' water \u0026quot;may no longer get treatment,\u0026quot; said Scott Faber, head of government affairs at the Environmental Working Group, an environmental health nonprofit based in Washington. Faber noted that PFAS treatment technologies remove other chemicals as well.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOnly 11\u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003estates have set their own\u0026nbsp;PFAS limits, so people in most of the country would be altogether without protections from these toxins.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eFederal limits on PFAS in drinking water\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEvery five years, the EPA requires water providers to test for about 30 contaminants, to gather data on where these contaminants are lurking and whether the government should regulate them. The samples are drawn from water after it has run through the treatment technologies the wells may have, similar to what comes out of taps.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eA previous round of sampling a decade ago led the EPA to adopt strict limits on six PFAS chemicals\u0026nbsp;in drinking water, alone or in combinations. For the\u0026nbsp;two\u0026nbsp;most studied ones,\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003ePFOA and PFOS, the federal limit is 4 parts per trillion; for the others the limit is 10 parts per trillion.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlthough these are very tiny concentrations — 1 part per trillion is the equivalent of roughly 30 seconds in a million years, or 7 square feet in the state of Texas — scientists have found long-term exposure to PFAS, even in tiny amounts, increases the risk of\u0026nbsp;prostate, kidney\u0026nbsp;and testicular cancers,\u0026nbsp;developmental problems in infants and children and other health problems. As the EPA noted in announcing the new regulation in April 2024, \u0026quot;there is no level of exposure to these contaminants without risk of health impacts, including certain cancers.\u0026quot; The EPA said the rule would reduce exposure for 100 million people\u0026nbsp;and \u0026quot;prevent thousands of deaths.\u0026quot;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn this round of sampling, providers are again testing for the six newly regulated compounds, as well as 23 unregulated PFAS, plus lithium. A Newsday analysis of the sampling published in April \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/environment/pfas-drinking-water-short-chain-hwchutiq\"\u003efound\u0026nbsp;19\u0026nbsp;Long Island water suppliers detected unregulated chemicals\u003c/a\u003e, which can be more\u0026nbsp;difficult to remove. There's no drinking water standard for these particular chemicals yet, because their health effects are still being studied by scientists, though water providers have already started to\u0026nbsp;test effective treatments for them.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMany Long Island water suppliers have been treating their water for PFAS for several years, usually with granular activated carbon systems, to comply with New York’s standard, which was established in 2020. That rule — the first state standard in the nation for PFAS in drinking water — set a limit for PFOA and PFOS at 10 parts per trillion.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe carbon systems — which work a bit like a huge Brita filter — effectively remove PFOA and PFOS to levels well below the state’s \u0026quot;maximum contaminant level.\u0026quot;\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome local water districts emphasize that once they start treating for PFAS, they aim to treat until the levels are undetectable. \u0026quot;When we see something, our goal is really to have nondetect everywhere,\u0026quot; said Tom Schneider, director of water quality at the Suffolk County Water Authority.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJoseph Corbisiero, director of plant operations at the Water Authority of Western Nassau, said whether the rule is 10 ppt or 4 ppt, \u0026quot;the ultimate goal is nondetect.\u0026quot;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStill, getting to zero or near zero requires suppliers to change the filtering medium more frequently, and that gets expensive.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003ePercent of readings above limit\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe EPA requires water districts to submit multiple samples from their wells over the course of a year, then gathers the individual readings and calculates annual average. The data collection continues through 2025, with a total of 44 Long Island water districts required to report.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOut of the \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/environment/pfas-test-results-database-br1c16z2\"\u003e36 districts that submitted data so far\u003c/a\u003e, 17 had at least one sample that tested above the maximum contaminant level for at least one of the chemicals. The great majority of the samples from Long Island tested below the federal standard. Out of 4,986 total samples submitted so far by Long Island water suppliers, only 70 tested above the federal limit, or 1.4%.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOne high reading could be an outlier,\u0026nbsp;but a high\u0026nbsp;annual average suggests a more persistent presence of a contaminant. So it's the annual average that the EPA will use to determine if a water supplier is in compliance with the limit.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe seven Long Island districts that had annual averages exceeding\u0026nbsp;the federal limit are\u0026nbsp;Garden City, Glen Cove, Locust Valley, Suffolk County Water Authority, Water Authority of Western Nassau, Westbury and Williston Park.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSeven out of 36 is just slightly above the national average\u0026nbsp;for similarly sized water districts — 19% versus 15%.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/aa67baaa-d0ca-4669-b5ff-1e8baaf89c5c\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/aa67baaa-d0ca-4669-b5ff-1e8baaf89c5c', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/aa67baaa-d0ca-4669-b5ff-1e8baaf89c5c\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPFAS250511_table\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSince those samples were taken, all the\u0026nbsp;water district managers who responded to Newsday's question said they've added treatment systems.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt the Suffolk County Water Authority, for example, a sample taken in 2023 at the Station Road well field had 17.4 parts per trillion\u0026nbsp;of PFOS, more than 4\u0026nbsp;times the federal limit.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAll three wells at that site now have granular activated carbon systems — the most recent were installed just last month, according to Jeff Szabo, CEO of the water authority.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome other wells in the district are due to have treatment systems\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003einstalled in the future, according to Schneider, the district's water quality director.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;We're very confident we'll be fully compliant long before 2029,\u0026quot; Szabo said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFifteen water districts reported individual readings above the federal limit of 4 parts per trillion but below the state standard of 10.\u0026nbsp;Should the federal regulations not go into effect, people served by those districts could be exposed to higher levels of PFOS and PFAS. However,\u0026nbsp;these districts that responded to Newsday also\u0026nbsp;said they have already installed treatment\u0026nbsp;systems on the wells that had high readings, or in some cases are designing or constructing treatment systems.
