that can be difficult to remove, according to a federal database of testing results, providing a look at a new challenge facing the Island’s drinking water.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe health effects of those chemicals, known as \u0026quot;short-chain PFAS,\u0026quot; have not yet been extensively studied. But anticipating future regulations,\u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003ewater providers from Bethpage to Hampton Bays are already trying to figure out new methods to remove the stubborn contaminants.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome water districts have been conducting pilot studies for several years to test different techniques’ effectiveness, trying to determine \u0026quot;what the next round of solutions looks like,\u0026quot; said James Neri, a spokesman for the Long Island Water Conference, a trade group for water suppliers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;Unfortunately we don’t know the silver bullet that takes care of all of them,\u0026quot; he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEvery five years, the\u0026nbsp;federal Environmental Protection Agency requires the country’s water providers to test for about 30 new contaminants\u0026nbsp;— a process the agency calls the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe samples are drawn from the water after it has been treated to accurately reflect the\u0026nbsp;quality of the water that is ultimately delivered to households. The goal is to gather information about how prevalent they are and whether they should be subject to federal regulations.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePast testing rounds led the EPA in April 2024 to establish limits on six PFAS chemicals in drinking water, individually or\u0026nbsp;in combination.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn 2023, water utilities began to look for 23 short-chain PFAS, cousins to those six regulated PFAS compounds;\u0026nbsp;sampling continues through 2025 and reporting is expected to be completed next year. And while water districts across Long Island have installed filtration systems to remove so-called legacy PFAS,\u0026nbsp;\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/east-williston-williston-park-water-hikes-khrzdppv\"\u003eraising water rates\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;to do so, studies have shown that these newer compounds are more difficult to remove.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAccording to a Newsday analysis of the latest federal data, 77 out of 452 wells that have submitted data so far — or 17% — had these unregulated PFAS in their drinking water above a minimum reporting level in at least one test.\u0026nbsp;The reporting levels seem absurdly small — generally between 2 and 8 parts per trillion, depending on the chemical, though one has a limit of 20 ppt. (One part per trillion is the equivalent of about 30 seconds in a million years, or a single drop in 20 Olympic-sized swimming pools.)\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAn\u0026nbsp;overwhelming number of tests did not detect contaminants, or detected them at such low levels they didn't have to be reported.\u0026nbsp;Out of 19,181 reported tests for unregulated PFAS, 203 readings were at or\u003cstrong\u003e \u003c/strong\u003eabove the minimum reporting level, or 1%.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/4b9be55a-7a81-451c-9a80-c67f35bc8394\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/4b9be55a-7a81-451c-9a80-c67f35bc8394', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/4b9be55a-7a81-451c-9a80-c67f35bc8394\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: liPFAS250420\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eHealth effects of short-chain PFAS being studied\u0026nbsp;\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStill, for those areas with relatively high readings, the results could be concerning.\u003cstrong\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/strong\u003eThere’s ample evidence that the health effects of the legacy PFAS compounds — particularly PFOA and PFOS — can be disproportionately large despite\u0026nbsp;low concentrations. Peer-reviewed scientific studies have found these chemicals accumulate in the body over time, and prolonged exposure\u0026nbsp;is associated with reduced immunity, thyroid disorders, developmental delays in children, kidney and liver disease and cancer, primarily kidney, breast and testicular cancer.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAnd there is some emerging evidence that the health risks of short-chain compounds could be similar. A \u003ca href=\"https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-03/GenX-Toxicity-Assessment-factsheet-March-2023-update.pdf\"\u003e2021 EPA report\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;notes animal studies show exposure to\u0026nbsp;one of the short-chain compounds results in health effects on\u0026nbsp;\u0026quot;the\u0026nbsp;liver, kidneys, the immune system, development of offspring, and an association with cancer.\u0026quot;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHuman studies\u0026nbsp;of\u0026nbsp;second-generation PFAS are underway but the long-term effects\u0026nbsp;\u0026quot;are largely still unknown,\u0026quot; according to Zeyan Liew, an environmental epidemiologist at Yale University’s School of Public Health. Short-chain PFAS, named because\u0026nbsp;they have fewer carbon atoms linked together, may not remain in the body as long as the long-chains, Liew wrote in an email to Newsday; but he said many other chemicals that leave the body relatively quickly can be harmful nevertheless.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAnother reason for concern is because PFAS are so prevalent, \u0026quot;we keep reexposing ourselves to a similar dose day after day,\u0026quot; said Erin Bell, an epidemiologist at the University at Albany, who is studying the long-term effects of PFAS-contaminated drinking water in upstate Hoosick Falls and Newburgh.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEnvironmental health advocates point out water is only one of many sources of contamination, along with things like food packaging and household products, including shampoo and even toilet paper.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;We’re already grossly overexposed,\u0026quot; said Scott Faber, senior vice president for government affairs at the Environmental Working Group.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat means it’s important to remove the chemical wherever possible, Faber added. \u0026quot;When we have a lever we can pull, we should pull it as hard as we can.\u0026quot;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEliminating the source of the contamination, experts say, would have tangible benefits for the environment and for human health.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;The good news is, when we reduce our exposure to these chemicals, the amount that is in our bodies will gradually go down,\u0026quot; Faber said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSince the monitoring began in 2023, 36 out of the 44 Long Island water providers required to collect and report samples have done so. Some districts are scheduled to submit results later; small districts and those using other districts’ water are not required to report.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eLong Island water districts testing new technologies\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eGranular activated carbon systems — which work like a giant household filter — can remove PFAS and other contaminants to non-detectable levels, and many Long Island water districts have already installed these on their wells.  Each one costs $1.5 million to $3 million, according to Neri, the water supplier spokesman who's also\u0026nbsp;director of engineering at Melville-based H2M architects + engineers.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe problem: The short-chain PFAS are not captured as efficiently by these filters.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;There are some small-chain compounds that can pass right through those media,\u0026quot; said Michelle Crimi, a professor of environmental and civil engineering at Clarkson University in upstate Potsdam.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eChanging the carbon in the vessels more frequently may be one solution, according to Mike Boufis, superintendent of the Bethpage Water District. To efficiently remove long-chain PFAS, the carbon ordinarily needs to be replaced after two or three years. For the short-chains, it might have to be swapped after just a few months.\u003cbr /\u003e \u0026quot;That's something that we are exploring now, just to see how quickly it breaks through carbon,\u0026quot; Boufis said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen the Hampton Bays Water District detected a short-chain PFAS at its Plant No. 1 wellfield in 2023, the carbon was replaced, according to James Kappers, the district’s superintendent. EPA data showed no PFAS in the next round of testing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBoufis predicted some water districts will start to use a different technology: ion exchange resins. Essentially, this method works by running water through a resin or polymer so that harmful ions are \u0026quot;exchanged\u0026quot; with harmless ones.  \u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBethpage has resin systems on two wells, installed to remove other contaminants, and is building another. Boufis said the resin technique removes some of the short-chain PFAS \u0026quot;but doesn't remove it 100%.” The district is experimenting \u0026quot;to find a specific resin\u0026quot; that works best.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIt’s hard to say how much such a system could cost, according to Neri, because \u0026quot;there are so many variables\u0026quot;: Each district and even each well may have a different combination of compounds.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCrimi, who is a member of the New York Drinking Water Quality Council, which sets state standards, said researchers are working to develop additional filtration methods that are \u0026quot;tuned for the smaller-chain compounds.\u0026quot;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThere’s no consensus yet on what method will be most efficient and cost-effective.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u0026quot;It's still in the infant stage, to be honest with you,\u0026quot; Boufis said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch2\u003eUncertain future for 'sins of the past'\u003c/h2\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAny federal regulation on these newer PFAS would be years away. Speaking to reporters April 11 in Woodbury, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin said the administration had not made any decisions on whether to maintain the limits set under President Joe Biden.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIf the EPA’s 4 parts per trillion\u0026nbsp;standard is eliminated, only New York state’s drinking water standard of 10 ppt for PFOA and PFOS will remain. Hakeem Jeffries (D-Brooklyn) said this week\u0026nbsp;that Democrats in that chamber will pass an Iran war powers resolution directing Trump to end the war during the first week of the new Congress in January, but there's no indication Trump would sign it or abide by that.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMeanwhile, current Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has panned proposals to stop or restrict war funding, describing it to\u0026nbsp;reporters last week as \"not a realistic ask\" which would complicate the talks on a bipartisan bill to keep government open.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The issue is how [a new funding bill]\u0026nbsp;gets done, what we can get done in the short term, and then, what we need to do afterward,\" Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Appropriations\u0026nbsp;Committee, told Newsday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eShe acknowledged some\u0026nbsp;Democrats \"have an appetite\" for using the leverage of\u0026nbsp;a potential government shutdown in order to stop war funding, but she\u0026nbsp;agreed\u0026nbsp;with Thune that those demands complicate\u0026nbsp;talks.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAs Gillibrand described it, \"We want to make sure that they don't pass a huge budget that has a ton of money for war funding,\" adding, \"We won't support it. But I think people are done with this war, so I don't know.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLong Island Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-Glen Cove) in a statement called for a \"bipartisan agreement that ends the war ... without shutting the government down.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRep. But Gillen said she believed \"the American people sent a very strong message, I think, to this administration that the war needs to end ... and that we need to have some resolution to the conflict.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLong Island’s two Republican congressmen said it would be a mistake for Democrats to force a shutdown.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Congress has a responsibility to provide oversight, but we cannot risk withholding pay from our troops or shutting down the government to force an outcome,\" Rep. The suit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York, calls for injunctive relief to stop Optimum from continuing its allegedly deceptive advertising that omits the network enhancement fee, alongside monetary damages.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Optimum continues to invest in our network, including bringing fiber internet to more than 3 million homes, and we give customers great value across our full suite of products,\" Optimum wrote in a statement to Newsday when asked about the class-action lawsuit. \"We take customer concerns seriously and remain focused on delivering the best possible experience.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOptimum Communications, formerly known as Altice USA, also operates News 12 Networks, including News 12 Long Island.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003ePotential classes\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe complaint has three claims for relief: one alleging violations of New York State law barring abusive business conduct, another alleging a violation of New York false advertising law, and a third alleging that Optimum has been unjustly enriched because of its alleged conduct.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe case has two potential defined classes; one for nationwide customers and one for New York customers. The two classes include all Optimum Internet customers who were charged a \"Network Enhancement Fee\" on or after Nov. 13, 2020.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe lawsuit is seeking class-action status, but no class has been certified and no settlement has been reached. Customers cannot file claims for compensation at this stage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMost class actions are opt-out cases, so consumers eligible for potential relief are automatically included unless they request to be excluded, according to the legal information website \u003ca href=\"https://www.classaction.org/\"\u003eClassAction.org\u003c/a\u003e. Once a case settles, class members must file a claim form online or by mail by the settlement deadline to receive compensation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eFee disclosures\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOptimum charges customers a mandatory \"network enhancement fee\" on top of the advertised monthly price for its internet service, according to the complaint. Optimum advertises to customers a flat monthly rate for internet services, the complaint states, but the company adds a $6 fee to customers' monthly bill separately from the monthly internet charge.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOptimum does not disclose the fee when customers purchase their services, Dichter's complaint alleges. The suit states that Dichter did not discover the fee until he received his monthly bill.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The only price that consumers consider and rely upon when conducting price comparisons with similar service providers is the internet service's advertised price,\" the complaint reads. \"Reasonable consumers cannot be expected to ferret out these hidden fees.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDichter is represented by a coalition of three law firms, New York City’s Reese LLP, Washington, D.C.'s KalielGold PLLC and Arkansas’ Jennings \u0026amp; Earley PLLC. None of the law firms responded to a Newsday request for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eConsumer impact\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsumers tend to anchor on the first price they see for a product, Columbia University Business School Professor\u003ca href=\"https://business.columbia.edu/faculty/people/vicki-morwitz\"\u003e Vicki G. Morwitz\u003c/a\u003e said in an interview with Newsday. Consumers are unlikely to change their buying decision after a hidden price is revealed, Morwitz said, often assuming that other internet providers will have similar charges.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eShe believes hidden fees make it harder for an honest business to compete, because they can appear more expensive than competitors that use additional hidden fees to artificially lower the monthly price.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe fee also allows Optimum to raise its prices while appearing to honor the original monthly cost, according to the complaint. Court documents allege that Optimum raised the network charge from $2.50 to $6, but the complaint does not specify when the increase occurred.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Consumers will be more willing to accept a price increase if it's hidden in a surcharge,\" Morwitz said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eClass-action status\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThis is not the first time Optimum’s billing practices have drawn scrutiny. Connecticut's attorney general filed a \u003ca href=\"https://portal.ct.gov/ag/press-releases/2024-press-releases/attorney-general-tong-files-suit-against-altice-over-unlawful-network-enhancement-fee\"\u003elawsuit in 2024\u003c/a\u003e against Optimum over the use of network enhancement fees, alleging they deceive customers. That case is still ongoing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOptimum settled a class-action lawsuit over network enhancement fees and other similar charges in 2023 in the Superior Court of New Jersey by creating a settlement fund worth up to $15 million, according to \u003ca href=\"https://truthinadvertising.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Seale-v-Altice-Settlement-Agreement.pdf\"\u003ecourt documents\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuccessful class-action lawsuits do not always lead to companies changing their behavior, co-director of the Case Western Reserve University Center for Business Law \u003ca href=\"https://case.edu/law/centers-institutes/business-law-center\"\u003eEric C. Chaffee\u003c/a\u003e said in an interview. A company may decide the profit from the alleged illegal activity is worth the cost of a class-action lawsuit, Chaffee said, and business people also may not realize that the alleged activity is unlawful.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"A lot of settlement agreements don't actually involve an acknowledgment of wrongdoing,\" Chaffee said. \"It may simply just be that one side has agreed to pay x number of dollars for this particular issue to go defendant will be sentenced to 18 years in state prison for second-degree kidnapping under an agreement with prosecutors, according to a transcript of the proceeding.","body":"\u003cp\u003eThe Bellport man accused of picking up a 14-year-old Long Island girl at the start of her weekslong disappearance in December 2024 has \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/missing-girl-east-patchogue-alton-harrell-sn2zu78p\"\u003epleaded guilty to rape\u003c/a\u003e and kidnapping charges, court records show.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlton Harrell, 37, will be sentenced to 18 years in state prison for second-degree kidnapping under an agreement with prosecutors, according to a transcript of the proceeding.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors said the plea deal will spare the victim from \"having to relive\" the abuse suffered at the hands of Harrell, who admitted Tuesday to \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/missing-girl-east-patchogue-grand-jury-indictment-kadft5xg\"\u003ehaving sex with the girl\u003c/a\u003e and providing her with drugs on multiple occasions despite knowing she was underage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk Assistant District Attorney Dana Castaldo called the girl, who Newsday is not naming because she is a minor and the victim of sex crimes, \"exceptionally vulnerable.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We do believe it is in her best interest to avoid her having to testify here with respect to the allegations against this defendant,\" the prosecutor told acting state Supreme Court Justice Karen Wilutis during the proceeding in Riverhead Tuesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHarrell had been facing the possibility of serving up to life in prison if convicted of first-degree kidnapping at trial.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDefense attorney Jeremy Scileppi, of Commack, told the judge the agreement was reached after he met with his client before the start of a scheduled pretrial hearing Tuesday morning. They had \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/alton-harrell-rejects-plea-offer-patchogue-girl-kidnapping-ykzu92j4\"\u003epreviously rejected\u003c/a\u003e an offer of 15 years to life in prison.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"He is of a mind that that is the way to resolve the case against him,\" Scileppi told the judge.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe defense attorney declined to offer additional comment after the plea.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors have said the girl’s 25-day ordeal began on Dec. 9, 2024, after she contacted Harrell, whom she had known since January 2024.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnder questioning from Castaldo on Tuesday, Harrell admitted meeting the girl when she was just 13 in January 2024 and that she told him at the time she was 14. Despite that, Harrell confirmed he picked up the girl at her father’s house in Patchogue that month and took her to a waterfront parking lot in Bellport, where he had sex with her and gave her crack cocaine.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHarrell also admitted returning to the home at 5 p.m. on the night she disappeared. He testified the girl was not wearing shoes or a coat and that she had a GPS monitoring bracelet she cut off while in his car. He admitted bringing her to an empty house in Bellport, where he had sex with her on an air mattress before leaving her there alone the next day after they came up with a plan for him to sell her jewelry for crack cocaine.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe girl left the house while Harrell was gone and was taken by another man to a motel in Bohemia.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCastaldo said at Harrell’s February 2025 arraignment that his actions in the first 24 hours of the girl’s disappearance \"set the entire chain of events that followed in motion.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt least seven other men were accused of raping the girl during her weekslong disappearance, including Francis Buckheit, the \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/missing-girl-sex-trafficking-rugegkjr\"\u003eowner of a yacht\u003c/a\u003e docked in Islip where the victim was discovered by her father on Jan. 3, 2025. The girl told police she stayed on the vessel with Buckheit for about three weeks.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHarrell admitted Tuesday to initially telling police he did not know where the girl was as they questioned him several times while she was still missing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn total, nine men and two women were indicted on kidnapping, rape, drug and child sex-trafficking charges related to the girl’s disappearance. Six defendants, including Buckheit, still face the possibility of going to trial on the indictment next year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors have said Harrell had no relationship with any other defendants in the case and is the only defendant who knew the girl before her disappearance.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSentencing is set for Jan. 14.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/085fd77e-48cb-412e-8e15-5df6920a10e0\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/085fd77e-48cb-412e-8e15-5df6920a10e0', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/085fd77e-48cb-412e-8e15-5df6920a10e0\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: limissing260407\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e","publishedDate":"2026-11-17T22:37:46.414Z","updatedDate":"2026-11-18T17:21:47.439Z","url":"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/long-island-missing-girl-alton-harrell-guilty-plea-dlr3f0c8","headline":"Bellport resident Alton Harrell pleads guilty to kidnapping and rape charges in missing girl case, court documents show","teaserTitle":"Man pleads guilty to rape and kidnapping charges in Long Island missing girl case, court documents show","newsLabel":"ndOnly","newsLabel2":"none","subType":"article","disableDeepLink":false,"moveAd":false,"textAudio":{"id":"contentid/e5bd08ba-266b-44b3-ac80-229734fd066a","title":"AIAudio - child for the year they all lived together.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The evidence presented to the grand jury in this case demonstrated that Barbara Renner played virtually no role in providing and/or caring for ​Jor'Dynn Duncan,\" Coysh wrote in the motion filed before State Supreme Court Justice John Collins in Riverhead. \"Not a single witness testified to Barbara Renner participating in any matters involving the schooling, supervision, discipline or general welfare of [the child].\"\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Barbara Renner, 75, was indicted on a said before kissing the girl in the first of the four videos. \"Come here my sweetheart, I need a little girl in my arms, I do, I need a little girl to love and you’re the one. Not just any little girl, I need you, I need you to be my little girl ... give me the hand ... I love you.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRizopoulos said that in each of the videos, which were recorded within eight minutes of each other, Jor'Dynn is \"not responsive.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"She seems barely conscious,\" the prosecutor wrote.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eGrand jury testimony from 30 witnesses\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e​Jor'Dynn was pronounced dead at NYU Langone Hospital-Suffolk in Patchogue at 11:47 a.m. on Dec. 29, roughly 75 minutes after Kelly and Renner alerted first responders to the child’s illness, court records show.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAn autopsy performed two days later by Suffolk County Medical Examiner Dr. Odette Hall determined ​Jor'Dynn had a perforated bowel and infected peritoneal cavity, injuries that were just days old at the time of her death. There were nine sharp-force injuries \"clustered in and around the anus,\" including a four-inch wound inside the anus that led to the perforated bowel and infection, according to the filing.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe medical examiner also reported older bruises, scars and contusions on her body and \"three to four\" bite marks on her right arm, leg and hand.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMuscatello, in her defense filing on behalf of Kelly, noted the autopsy revealed the injuries could have been caused by kitchen scissors. The attorney noted that Hall could not say for certain if Jor'Dynn would have survived had she gotten prompt medical attention.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMuscatello also argued the evidence prosecutors have shared suggests Kelly sought help from her mother and treated her with pain relief medication and an antihistamine, acts \"not consistent with a wanton, cruel and callous disregard for her life.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLoTurco said in his statement that he may also seek a change of venue, saying \"publicity has significantly prejudiced Ms. Kelly’s ability to obtain a fair trial in Suffolk County.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"These requests reflect our continuing commitment to protecting Ms. Kelly’s rights and ensuring that the proceedings against her are fair and based on legally sufficient evidence,\" LoTurco said. \"We respectfully await the Court’s determination of the pending motion.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCourt records show Suffolk detectives first questioned Kelly, Renner and Kelly's daughter Elyssa Seymore the day of ​Jor'Dynn's death.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAn evidentiary notice filed by prosecutors shows the women made additional statements to law enforcement in January and February.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThey were arrested on May 20 after being indicted by a grand jury that saw 122 exhibits and heard testimony from 30 witnesses spanning more than 650 pages, court records show.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"So this is how we’re doing this?\" records show Kelly told law enforcement the day she was arrested on charges of depraved indifference murder, reckless endangerment, unlawful imprisonment and endangering the welfare of a child. Seymore was charged with unlawful imprisonment and endangering the welfare of the child for her role in alleged abuse that occurred months before ​Jor'Dynn's death, according to the indictment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSeymore's attorney, Katherine Fernandez, said she intends to file a separate motion on behalf of her client in the coming days. Her case is on the court's calendar for Tuesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAmong those who testified before the grand jury were teachers, counselors, school nurses and administrators with the Bayport-Blue Point school district. Prosecutors have said school officials described ​Jor'Dynn as a \"child that \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/investigations/jordynn-duncan-emily-kelly-bayport-blue-point-school-district-u3c0droi\"\u003elit up the room\u003c/a\u003e.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Smart. Intelligent. Kind. And very well-behaved,\" Rizopoulos said of the word’s school officials used to describe ​Jor'Dynn to police.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen officials with the school district, where ​Jor'Dynn had been enrolled to attend second grade, contacted the family with concerns over 40 absences in six months, Kelly offered different explanations for her absences, prosecutors previously said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eShe had illnesses, they reported at times, a death in the family another. Once Kelly said they took a trip to Disney World.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors have said none of those claims were true.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eA shift in blame\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eKelly, Renner and Seymore offered police a different explanation for ​Jor'Dynn's injuries: self-harm.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn statements to police included in court filings obtained by Newsday, including a sworn deposition \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/investigations/7-year-old-death-torture-death-jordynn-duncan-emily-kelly-szazk1fq\"\u003eKelly gave to police\u003c/a\u003e an hour after the girl’s death, the women told investigators ​Jor'Dynn began to have \"mental health issues\" after losing contact with her biological mother, Portia Duncan, in July 2025.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"She began to exhibit signs of depression,\" Kelly told police of Jor'Dynn. \"She would make herself throw up and began defecating on herself.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eKelly said on one occasion she caught the girl placing a household item \"in her rectum.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEven before the child died, Renner told first responders in an interaction captured at 10:40 a.m. by a police body camera that ​Jor'Dynn had \"been doing things to hurt herself.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePortia Duncan lost custody of her daughter at 14 months due to a failed drug test, according to a notice of claim she filed against Suffolk County, the school district and other entities for allegedly failing to adequately monitor the girl before her death.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e​Jor'Dynn spent most of her childhood in the care of her father’s former wife, Kim Jackson, court records show. She was removed from Jackson’s home in October 2024 after she was found to be spending unsupervised time with Duncan, prosecutors alleged in a summary of the case contained in the recent filings. Kelly's attorneys stated in their recent filing that the removal from Jackson's home came after Jor'Dynn, then 6, witnessed Duncan \"break somebody's head open with a baseball bat,\" citing grand jury testimony.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eKelly, who is engaged to ​Jor'Dynn's father, Derrick Dixon, obtained full guardianship in spring 2025 and told police Duncan \"disappeared\" from the child’s life after seeing her on the Fourth of July and having phone contact with her later that month.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAttempts by Newsday to contact Dixon, who was released from prison last month, were unsuccessful.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt a news conference in July, Duncan, who has since been arrested on new misdemeanor drug charges for which she is scheduled to be arraigned later this month, said she had been an addict, but was also \"a damn good mother.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Here I am, supposed to protect my daughter, and leaving her to be protected by Child Protective Services and she wasn’t protected,\" Duncan told reporters at her lawyer’s office in Melville. Duncan's civil attorney, Heather Palmore, said she had not seen the motions filed in the criminal case and did not offer comment when reached by a Newsday reporter Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eEfforts to hide the alleged abuse\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors, in court appearances and filings, have said the police investigation revealed photographic evidence of alleged abuse by Kelly and Seymore and text messages of them discussing it. The autopsy noted the bite marks on Jor'Dynn's body were not consistent with \"self-harm,\" court records show.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Elyssa Seymore, 24, Renner has sought to have charges of manslaughter and child endangerment dropped. Renner's attorney has said Renner has dementia.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors have said there was a \"dysfunctional family relationship\" at the small Oak Street home that the women shared. Kelly called 911 and reported that Jor'Dynn was in cardiac arrest. Paramedics found the girl unconscious on the floor outside a bathroom in the three-bedroom home and took her to NYU Langone Hospital-Suffolk in Patchogue, where she was pronounced dead about an hour later.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAn autopsy of Jor'Dynn that was performed two days later showed that she suffered a perforated bowel and infected peritoneal cavity, injuries that were only days old at the time of her death. That period coincided with Emily Kelly, the woman accused of her murder, gaining permanent custody of Jor'Dynn.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday reported earlier this year that Suffolk County Child Protective Services conducted \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/investigations/jordynn-duncan-emily-kelly-suffolk-cps-b6728ytc\"\u003eno investigations\u003c/a\u003e into Jor’Dynn’s care in the year before her death, meaning the agency received no credible allegations of abuse or neglect during that time from school staff or anyone else.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Any reasonable person can look at that and see that there's something wrong here,\" Heather Palmore, an attorney representing Jor’Dynn’s mother, Portia Duncan, told Newsday of the newly disclosed absences.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSchool officials are required to report suspicions of abuse and neglect to child welfare authorities, including educational neglect, which can be triggered by chronic absences.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut the State of New York \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/investigations/jordynn-duncan-emily-kelly-bayport-blue-point-school-district-u3c0droi\"\u003edoes not require districts\u003c/a\u003e to take any specific action over repeated absences. The state Education Department has increasingly encouraged districts to involve Child Protective Services \"as a tool of last resort,\" a spokesperson told Newsday earlier this year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePortia Duncan filed a \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/jordynn-duncan-death-suffolk-county-notice-of-claim-lvhn5xtn\" target=\"_blank\"\u003enotice of claim\u003c/a\u003e in July signaling her intent to sue Suffolk County and the school district, among others, for allegedly failing to ensure the girl's safety\u0026nbsp;before she died. Duncan is seeking $250 million in damages, though the lawsuit has not yet been filed.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"The school was clearly on notice,\" Palmore said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Bayport-Blue Point school district declined to comment on Jor’Dynn’s absences from Academy Street Elementary or on any action the district took related to them, citing privacy rights and the pending litigation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFormer Bayport-Blue Point Superintendent Timothy Hearney, who retired in July and now serves as principal of a Catholic school in Huntington, did not respond to a request for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Suffolk County medical examiner determined Jor’Dynn died of an infection caused by a perforated colon. She was found with 90 recent injuries, including nine inflicted by \"sharp force\" and three or four bite marks that an expert determined were not self-inflicted.\u003c/p\u003e this month about the alleged treatment of Jor’Dynn, saying in court filings that Kelly, her daughter Elyssa Seymore and Kelly’s mother, Barbara Renner, left the girl alone at their Bayport home for a full day.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAttorneys for Kelly, who is engaged to Jor’Dynn’s father, and Seymore did not respond to requests for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAn attorney for World.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe recently filed court records showed that Kelly would respond via the school messaging application regarding the 18 absences between September 2025 and December the dozens of missed days the previous school year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJor’Dynn’s godmother, Alisha Case, told Newsday she has been \"shocked\" by the lack of documentation for Jor’Dynn’s dinner for 10 people is\u0026nbsp;$58.63, a 6.3% increase from 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation, a Washington, D.C.-based trade group.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIt’s the first centerpiece of many Thanksgiving tables, had the biggest price increase among the items in the survey and was the largest driver of the overall increase, according to the federation, which released its 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner survey results\u0026nbsp;Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe average price of a 16-pound frozen turkey is $23.68, or $1.48 per pound, a 10% increase from last year, the trade group reported.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“The overall increase in our annual survey reflects the rising costs of getting food from the farm to your dinner table,” the Turkey prices rose 10% nationwide from last Thanksgiving, the largest increase among the items surveyed by the American Farm Bureau Federation.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe federation’s price data is based on surveys conducted by volunteer shoppers who checked prices in stores and online in the first week of November.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAmong the 12 items on the grocery list, prices for eight products increased, including a 30-ounce can of pumpkin pie mix, up 1.9% to $4.24; a gallon of whole milk, up 8.6% to $4.05; one dozen dinner rolls, up 7% to $3.81; and three pounds of sweet potatoes, up 5% to $4.20.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/bd046e18-07c7-413d-b38d-b87a437581bf\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/bd046e18-07c7-413d-b38d-b87a437581bf', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/bd046e18-07c7-413d-b38d-b87a437581bf\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: bzthanksgiving261128_chart2\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAmong the products with falling prices were a 1-pound tray of carrots and celery, down 3.7% to $1.31; two frozen pie crusts, down 2.7% to $3.28; and a half-pint of whipping cream, down 1.6% to $1.84.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe federation also calculated the cost of an expanded Thanksgiving meal that includes boneless ham, russet potatoes and frozen green beans. That meal averaged $81.72, up 6% from last year.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/34077aa5-2bca-4eb9-978c-96deca4e07e2\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/34077aa5-2bca-4eb9-978c-96deca4e07e2', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/34077aa5-2bca-4eb9-978c-96deca4e07e2\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: bzThanksgiving261119_chart3\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSeveral factors are pushing holiday food costs higher, including increased fuel expenses for harvesting and transportation, the federation reported.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003cstrong\u003e\u003c/strong\u003eMeanwhile, turkey prices are up as production costs rise and supplies remain tight, despite the U.S.\u0026nbsp;turkey industry now recovering\u0026nbsp;after two years of shrinking supplies due to disease-related bird losses, the trade group reported.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhat's driving up food prices\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"Canned pumpkin products line a shelf at Holiday Farms in Franklin Square ahead of Thanksgiving. Eight of the 12 items in the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual holiday meal survey increased in price this year.\" data-attr-credit=\"Newsday\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/965557d3-4b19-4c81-b885-e879f8f3398e\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/965557d3-4b19-4c81-b885-e879f8f3398e', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/965557d3-4b19-4c81-b885-e879f8f3398e\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/965557d3-4b19-4c81-b885-e879f8f3398e/2O0A0599.jpg?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eCanned pumpkin products line a shelf at Holiday Farms in Franklin Square ahead of Thanksgiving. Eight of the 12 items in the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual holiday meal survey increased in price this year.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn the 25-county region\u0026nbsp;that includes Long Island, overall grocery prices in October 2026 were 30.1% higher than in October 2019, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Food prices are high right now. They remain elevated from COVID and the aftermath, and there’s been no relief,” said Ricky Volpe, an agricultural economics professor at California Polytechnic State University.\u0026nbsp;He said grocery price increases this year have outpaced consumers’ wage gains.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eGrocery prices nationwide rose 0.4% between September and October, “which is a pretty big monthly jump,” said Volpe, adding that monthly increases between 0.1% to 0.2% are more average.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHigher energy costs, mostly from\u0026nbsp;diesel, are the biggest factor in food price hikes overall this year, not just for Thanksgiving, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe conflict in Iran, which began Feb. 28, has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil shipments, adding pressure to fuel costs.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Diesel is a source of energy that is absolutely crucial to the food supply chain. It's used in various forms for harvesting, processing, storage, transportation. It's one of the major sort of lifeblood, you know, commodities of the entire food system,” Volpe said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn 2022, grocery prices rose at rates not seen since the 1970s amid higher commodity and production costs, including pressures tied to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Avian influenza also contributed to poultry losses, with millions of birds dying from the disease or being euthanized. Others could shop for a new term policy.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsumers could buy permanent life insurance or convert their term policy to permanent coverage, if their policy includes that option.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThey also could opt to let the policy expire and take\u0026nbsp;on the financial risk of an untimely death using their own assets and investments.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe right decision is dependent on a person’s financial circumstances, age and comfort with risk, said David Frisch, CEO of Frisch Financial Group in Melville.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut some Long Islanders might be weighing the cost of life insurance against essential needs like paying for heating oil and may choose to postpone a purchase, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Each family’s decision is very personal,” Frisch said. “Some families are going to say, ‘No matter what it costs to protect my family, I'm willing to pay that price.’ \"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe percentage of Americans with a life insurance policy, including coverage through their employer, has long been declining and dropped\u0026nbsp;to 52% this year from 60% in 2016. That's\u0026nbsp;according to data from LIMRA, a Windsor, Connecticut-based life insurance industry trade association.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/88902d68-20f7-4a15-94ec-7ca1c3f3098e\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/88902d68-20f7-4a15-94ec-7ca1c3f3098e', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/88902d68-20f7-4a15-94ec-7ca1c3f3098e\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: bzLIFE261119_fever chart\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome of the factors contributing to the decline include younger generations getting married and having their first child later, according to LIMRA.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsumers also face\u0026nbsp;competing financial priorities including paying off student loan debt and \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/real-estate/buying-selling-house-long-island-hltoavvz\"\u003esaving for a house,\u003c/a\u003e said Karen Terry, director of LIMRA Insurance Research.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut ownership has risen since the pandemic, she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Anything that's going to raise people's awareness of their own mortality is going to raise interest in a product like insurance,” she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFinancial planners and life insurance experts who spoke with Newsday weighed the pros and cons of those options, explained key concepts consumers need to know and discussed mistakes to avoid.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eShould consumers\u0026nbsp;renew their term policy or buy a new policy?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe first question policyholders should ask is why they purchased coverage in the first place, Frisch said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCommon reasons to buy life insurance include paying for childcare, mortgage expenses or college costs, he said. If those expenses are still a factor, some individuals might purchase another term policy.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut consumers should be aware that renewing a term policy in your 50s or buying a new one can be significantly more expensive, said Craig Ferrantino, president of Craig James Financial Services in Melville.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/81f812ad-107c-4f3d-bab8-27fa7a1e0bf9\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/81f812ad-107c-4f3d-bab8-27fa7a1e0bf9', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" does coverage get as you age?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOne analysis by personal finance website NerdWallet found the average rate quote was 3.8 times higher for a male 50-year-old and 3.5 times higher for a female 50-year-old when compared with a 30-year-old of the same gender.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThose quotes were for nonsmokers in good health seeking a 20-year term life insurance policy with $500,000 in coverage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHowever, rates can vary widely based on a person’s health, family medical history, driving record and the risk of their occupation, \u003ca href=\"https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/life/learn/what-is-term-life-insurance\"\u003eNerdWallet data shows\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/81f812ad-107c-4f3d-bab8-27fa7a1e0bf9\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/81f812ad-107c-4f3d-bab8-27fa7a1e0bf9', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/81f812ad-107c-4f3d-bab8-27fa7a1e0bf9\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: bzLIFE261119_column chart\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome carriers offer life insurance without a medical exam, but those policies have higher annual premiums on average, according to NerdWallet.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhat are the pros and cons of opting for term versus permanent insurance?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTerm life insurance offers a cheaper option for younger consumers to protect against an early demise. The policy has no cash value and only pays out if a person dies during the term, according to NerdWallet.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhole life insurance, \u003ca href=\"https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/life/learn/term-vs-whole-life-insurance\"\u003eone type\u003c/a\u003e of permanent insurance, is more expensive but builds cash value over time that could be borrowed against in the future.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/c31a06e4-dd54-4f2a-a57c-4084134cf9bf\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/c31a06e4-dd54-4f2a-a57c-4084134cf9bf', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/c31a06e4-dd54-4f2a-a57c-4084134cf9bf\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: bzLIFE261119_bar chart\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe goal of permanent insurance is often geared toward leaving an inheritance, protecting a surviving spouse or covering taxes on wealth transfers to beneficiaries, Frisch said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFerrantino said he encourages term life insurance buyers to pay a\u0026nbsp;higher premium for a policy that has a rider allowing them to convert it to permanent insurance at the end of the term. That can protect policyholders in the event they're diagnosed with a serious health condition.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“You're taking a risk of not being able to be insured or being insured at a different rate” that’s typically higher as you age, he said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eHow much coverage does a person need?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFidelity Investments recommends buying coverage worth 10 to 12 times your annual income. But the company describes several approaches to tailor that guideline to a person’s needs.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOne method involves multiplying annual income by the number of years your family would need financial support, \u003ca href=\"https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/personal-finance/how-much-life-insurance-do-I-need\"\u003eaccording to Fidelity\u003c/a\u003e. Another focuses on obligations, such as debt and living expenses.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe purpose of life insurance is to transfer the financial risk from one's family\u0026nbsp;to the insurance company, Frisch said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eA person might forego buying another policy, he said, if they determine they have adequate assets to cover the financial risk to their family or if they opt to direct money toward other investments.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhat mistakes should you avoid?\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen buying insurance to replace an expiring policy, it’s best not to wait until the last minute, Frisch said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStarting the process before a policy lapses allows consumers to compare the potential cost of staying with a current insurer or selecting a new policy.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLife insurance buyers can be particularly vulnerable to this type of decision paralysis, Frisch said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e“Dealing with mortality of any kind — whether it's death, disability, going into a nursing home — it's a very emotional topic, and sometimes people just don't want to deal with it,” Frisch said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsumers should also avoid missing a payment that could put them at risk of termination, typically after a grace period, Ferrantino said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMost carriers allow for reinstatement during a certain time period if you make back payments plus interest, \u003ca href=\"https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-happens-if-you-stop-paying-life-insurance-premiums/\"\u003eaccording to Experian.\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e","publishedDate":"2026-11-18T10:00:00Z","updatedDate":"2026-11-18T05:21:52.574Z","url":"https://www.newsday.com/business/wallet-watch/term-life-insurance-options-cy6uwuip","headline":"Life insurance expiring? costs.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEmployers nationwide are expecting the biggest increase in healthcare expenses since 2003 — 8.2% — according to \u003ca href=\"https://www.mercer.com/en-us/insights/us-health-news/survey-health-benefit-costs-expected-to-jump-in-2027/ \"\u003ea survey of businesses\u003c/a\u003e with 50 or more employees by the Manhattan-based consulting firm Marsh. That increase would have been 11% if companies hadn’t found ways to reduce expenses.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMany businesses that previously had been reluctant to pass on the full cost of annual insurance premium increases to workers are now doing so, said Beth Umland, director of health research for Marsh.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSome companies are trimming the share of premium costs\u0026nbsp;they cover — for example, reducing the\u0026nbsp;80% of employees’ premiums, a common percentage,\u0026nbsp;to a lower proportion in\u0026nbsp;2027, Umland said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Their hand has sort of been forced with trends of this size,\" she said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCosts for Affordable Care Act plans are rising even more, \u003ca href=\"https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/9-things-to-watch-for-the-2027-aca-open-enrollment-period/\"\u003ea median of 13% for mid-level plans,\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;as are prices for Medicare Part D premiums, which cover prescription drugs and are expected to \u003ca href=\"https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-part-d-premiums-and-cost-sharing-in-2027/\"\u003espike by an average of 50%\u003c/a\u003e,\u0026nbsp;assuming that policyholders keep their current plans, according to analyses by the health research and policy nonprofit KFF.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePremiums for small-business plans that Melville insurance agent Matthew Caselli handles are increasing by an average of about 4% to 6%. But, he said, some insurers have dropped low-premium plans, forcing businesses to choose from more expensive options.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I’ve seen increases of up to 60%\" after businesses'\u0026nbsp;low-premium policies were excised, said Caselli, president of Eagle Group Planning. \"Products are being streamlined, and they’re eliminating less profitable plans.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eDifficult choices\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCompanies often are choosing plans with higher deductibles and employee copays, Caselli said. More businesses also are buying \"non-traditional products,\" such as ones that allow small companies to pool together to form a larger insurance plan, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThat is what Chris Dara, a client of Caselli and owner of IT in Demand in Huntington, an IT support company with five employees, plans to do in 2027.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBuying a traditional group insurance plan \"is unattainable,\" Dara said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Affordable Care Act requires companies of 50 or more employees to provide health insurance\u0026nbsp;or face a penalty. Smaller businesses are exempt. Only about 23% of businesses with fewer than 10 employees, and 52% of those with 10-24 employees, offer health coverage, according to 2023 data \u003ca href=\"https://www.ebri.org/content/new-research-finds-percentage-of-small-employers-offering-health-benefits-in-decline-but-employment-based-health-coverage-still-most-common-source-of-health-coverage-for-nonelderly-population\"\u003eanalyzed by the Washington, D.C.-based Employee Benefits Research Institute\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWaxman \u0026amp; Bland, a Melville accounting firm, provides coverage for its six employees despite the cost and lack of legal requirement in part because \"we’re competing for employees against some incredibly large accounting firms that have a more robust benefit package than we do,\" said Frank Bland, managing partner of the company. Some pay 100% of the cost of premiums, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We just can’t do that,\" so his firm offers flexibility in time off and work schedules\u0026nbsp;to help compete, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe state caps rate increases for plans that it regulates. State-regulated small-group plans for businesses with 100 or fewer employees will increase an average 8% in 2027, with the amount varying by company, and individual plans will increase an average of 6%, \u003ca href=\"https://myportal.dfs.ny.gov/fr/web/prior-approval/ind-and-sg-medical/summary-of-2027-requested-rate-actions \"\u003eaccording to the Department of Financial Services, which approved the price hikes\u003c/a\u003e. Both figures are much less than insurers had requested, the state said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIncreases in healthcare costs have long \u003ca href=\"https://www.healthsystemtracker.org/brief/how-does-medical-inflation-compare-to-inflation-in-the-rest-of-the-economy/\"\u003eoutpaced the overall inflation rate\u003c/a\u003e: Between 2000 and 2024, medical spending rose more than 121%, compared with an 86% increase in the price of goods and services overall, according to a KFF analysis of federal data.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It’s difficult to say what turns the tide,\" said Sunit Patel, chief actuary for Marsh U.S. Health.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOne potential way to control costs in the future is efficiencies from increased use of artificial intelligence, Patel said. In addition, he said, some medications, such as\u0026nbsp;GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, may reduce healthcare costs over time, especially if the price of the medications continues to fall, because the savings yielded by the health benefits of the\u0026nbsp;drugs may outweigh their costs. \u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWeight-loss drugs\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe continued popularity of GLP-1s is a key factor in the 2027 increase in health costs, he said. Some employers have stopped covering GLP-1s other than for diabetes, or they’re requiring that those who take the medications participate in coaching programs designed to increase effectiveness, Umland said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOther pricey medications and very expensive new treatments —\u0026nbsp;some gene therapies cost millions of dollars —\u0026nbsp;also are contributing to rising costs, Patel said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsolidation of healthcare systems, which increases their bargaining power with insurers, is another factor, Umland and Patel found in their Marsh analysis. On Long Island, there no longer is an independent hospital other than the public Nassau University Medical Center, and a rising number of outpatient practices now affiliate with large health systems.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe same factors pushing up healthcare costs overall are increasing the prices of ACA plans, said Matt McGough, a policy analyst in KFF’s ACA program.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAnother key reason\u0026nbsp;is the Republican-controlled Congress’ decision to reduce or eliminate tax credits in 2026 for ACA policies for many middle and upper middle income families. Democrats have vowed to restore the subsidies when they assume the majority in January, but President Donald Trump, who supported reduced\u0026nbsp;subsidies, could veto any legislation.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePeople with lower incomes who make too much to qualify for Medicaid still receive large tax credits. But many who lost subsidies, or who now only qualify for much smaller ones,\u0026nbsp;saw huge increases in premiums, leading many younger, healthier people to forgo insurance, McGough said. Older, sicker people are more likely to maintain coverage,\u0026nbsp;he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe result is that a higher percentage of people in these ACA plans have health problems and high medical expenses. McGough said insurers\u0026nbsp;are \"going to increase premiums to compensate for that.\"\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/2e4e98d5-66e0-44ef-9e69-50f2359b3bd5","title":"AIAudio - Health insurance costs to jump in 2027 on Long Island\n","headline":"AIAudio - Health insurance costs to jump in 2027 on Long Island","mediaLink":null,"premiumType":"inherit","url":"https://www.newsday.com/news/health/aiaudio-health-insurance-costs-to-jump-in-2027-on-long-island-hfsdm8qm","updatedDate":null,"publishedDate":null,"newsLabel":null,"audioUrl":"https://api.newsday.atexcloud.io//file-delivery-service/version/c:ZWYwYTZkNTktZjYzOC00:ODc5MjVjNGEtMzE5Mi00/audio%2F36dd56d2-5922-45a9-bb4c-343630fa6e99.mp3","tags":[],"source":[],"contentPath":[{"id":"contentid/Newsday.News.d","title":"News","path":"/news","__typename":"Section"},{"id":"contentid/Newsday.News.Health.d","title":"Health","path":"/news/health","__typename":"Section"},{"id":"contentid/2e4e98d5-66e0-44ef-9e69-50f2359b3bd5","title":"AIAudio - Health insurance costs to jump in 2027 on Long Island\n","path":"/news/health/aiaudio-health-insurance-costs-to-jump-in-2027-on-long-island-hfsdm8qm","__typename":"Audio"}],"topElement":null,"__typename":"Audio"},"topElement":{"__typename":"Image","id":"contentid/ee379838-cfa9-485e-870b-64375605b525","width":2100,"height":1400,"title":"Copy Of LIINSURANCE261115_photos","headline":"","baseUrl":"https://cdn.newsday.com/image-service/version/c:NzE4ZGUwNWYtMTRlMS00:MDk1YTY0NDItNDM1NC00/copy-of-liinsurance261115_photos.","caption":"\u003cp\u003eMatthew A. What to know before choosing a new one.","body":"\u003cp\u003eSeniors across Long Island are navigating a choice that will determine their health coverage and costs in 2027: which Medicare plan to choose. Plans can vary widely in costs, benefits and doctor networks, while suspicious phone calls and aggressive sales tactics can further muddy the waters.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eRoughly 33,000 Medicare beneficiaries on Long Island will have their \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/health/medicare-advantage-emqadmhv\"\u003eplans discontinued for 2027\u003c/a\u003e, according to the Centers for Medicare \u0026amp; Medicaid Services. They have until Dec. 7, the end of Medicare's annual open enrollment period, to choose new coverage that takes effect Jan. 1.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBrian Krantz, founder of Plan Medicare, a Melville-based insurance brokerage that helps people compare and enroll in Medicare plans, said he's fielding a steady stream of calls from people looking for new coverage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I have to speak to someone every half-hour who is trying to find a new plan,\" Krantz said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePeople whose Medicare Advantage plans are discontinued will \u003ca href=\"https://www.forbes.com/sites/dianeomdahl/2026/10/22/your-medicare-advantage-plan-is-going-away-what-do-you-do-now/\"\u003eautomatically return to original Medicare\u003c/a\u003e if they don't choose another Advantage plan before their coverage ends. But they may need separate prescription drug coverage or supplemental insurance. Those whose Medicare Advantage or prescription drug plans aren't renewed also qualify for a special enrollment period extending through Feb. 28, according to Medicare.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eEven people whose plans are continuing should compare their options. Monthly premiums, deductibles, prescription coverage and access to doctors can vary significantly — and the cheapest plan isn't necessarily the least expensive in the long run.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConsumer advocates also warn that confusion over Medicare coverage can leave seniors vulnerable to scams and misleading sales pitches.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eMedicare scams: Horan, of Senior Health Plan Specialists Inc., discusses Medicare coverage options at the Smithtown Library last month.\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMaría Alvarez, executive director of the New York StateWide Senior Action Council, a nonprofit that advocates for older adults and helps them navigate Medicare, said scammers often exploit the confusion and pressure around open enrollment to steal personal information.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlvarez described a case in which Medicare numbers belonging to Long Islanders were used to order catheters they neither needed nor requested. \u003ca href=\"https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/consumer-alerts/consumer-alert-catheter-scam/\"\u003eFederal health officials have also\u003c/a\u003e warned of scams involving fraudulent charges for urinary catheters and other medical supplies.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOther Medicare fraud schemes involve fraudulent prescription drug claims.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn Nassau County, police recently charged two pharmacies — RNJ Pharmacy Inc. of Freeport and Jericho Express Rx Inc. of Floral Park — with healthcare fraud, grand larceny and identity theft.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eInvestigators allege the pharmacies submitted about $8 million in claims for high-cost medications, including claims involving Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers, and received roughly $5 million in payments. The medications were never dispensed, and the claims were submitted without the knowledge or consent of doctors and patients, \u003ca href=\"https://www.pdcn.org/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=15412\"\u003eaccording to Nassau County police.\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNassau police \u0026nbsp;said they are forming a task force to investigate similar schemes.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTo protect themselves, seniors should safeguard their Medicare numbers and avoid sharing them with unsolicited callers, Alvarez said. They should also review their Medicare claims for services or equipment they never received, \u003ca href=\"https://www.cms.gov/files/document/medicare-oep-marketing-guidelines-2026.pdf\"\u003eaccording to federal guidance\u003c/a\u003e. Beneficiaries can check claims at Medicare.gov and report suspected fraud to 1-800-MEDICARE.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"These things can happen all year 'round; it’s just not during the annual enrollment period,\" Alvarez said. \"This is a very important time of the year where people are conscious of all of these issues, so the scam artists pile on.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eDon't let extra perks distract from gaps in coverage\u003c/h3\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-attr-caption=\"An attendee reviews information about Medicare coverage changes during the Smithtown Library seminar. Credit: Barry Sloan\" data-attr-credit=\"\" data-attr-has-caption=\"true\" data-attr-has-credit=\"true\" data-attr-q=\"0.3\" data-attr-w=\"400\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/994b7016-3197-42c5-a707-c67365cd6809\" data-onecms-type=\"image\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/994b7016-3197-42c5-a707-c67365cd6809', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/994b7016-3197-42c5-a707-c67365cd6809\"\u003e\u003cimg src=\"/image-service/alias/contentid/994b7016-3197-42c5-a707-c67365cd6809/obj15321946_11904?w=400\u0026amp;q=0.3\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"captionwrapper\" style=\"display: block;\"\u003eAn attendee reviews information about Medicare coverage changes during the Smithtown Library seminar. Credit: Barry Sloan\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eChanges to federal marketing rules have raised concerns among consumer advocates about whether seniors have enough information to evaluate sales pitches. The changes were made to align with White House directives to simplify federal regulations, according to Centers for Medicare \u0026amp; Medicaid Services officials.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAlvarez said the changes could further complicate health insurance decisions.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnder federal rules finalized in April and in effect for this fall's enrollment, insurance agents and brokers selling Medicare plans through third-party marketing organizations no longer have to disclose how many insurers and plans they represent within the first minute of a sales call. They must still provide that information before discussing plan benefits. The required disclosure also no longer directs consumers to free state-run Medicare counseling programs, \u003ca href=\"https://www.cms.gov/files/document/medicare-oep-marketing-guidelines-2026.pdf\"\u003eaccording to CMS.\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.aarp.org/medicare/new-medicare-marketing-broker-rules/\"\u003eAARP opposed the changes\u003c/a\u003e, warning they could weaken consumer protections and make it harder for seniors to make informed coverage decisions.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, a trade group representing insurance agents and brokers, \u003ca href=\"https://nabip.org/media/10759/nabip-comment-letter_january-26-2026_cms-4208-p.pdf\"\u003esupported the change in a letter to CMS\u003c/a\u003e, arguing it would reduce confusion without weakening consumer protections. The group also called for stronger oversight of companies generating misleading Medicare sales leads.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eKrantz warned that unscrupulous brokers and insurance companies may emphasize incentives such as gym memberships while giving less attention to which doctors and hospitals a plan covers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It's really not fair that there are so many brokers and so many companies out there who are not playing by the book,\" Krantz said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eOriginal Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage: What you'll pay and what's covered\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOne of the biggest decisions facing beneficiaries is whether to choose original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. The options differ in cost, access to doctors and rules governing care.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMedicare is the federal health insurance program primarily for people 65 and older, though some younger people with disabilities or certain medical conditions also qualify.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eOriginal Medicare, administered by the federal government, includes hospital coverage under Part A and doctors' services and outpatient care under Part B. Beneficiaries can generally see any provider who accepts Medicare. But original Medicare has deductibles and other cost-sharing requirements, with no annual out-of-pocket limit for Part A and B services. Many people buy supplemental coverage, known as Medigap, to help pay those costs, along with a separate Part D prescription drug plan.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMedicare Advantage, offered by private insurers, often has lower monthly premiums and includes drug coverage. But plans typically limit patients to networks of doctors and hospitals and may require prior authorization for some services. Preferred provider organizations, or PPOs, generally cover some out-of-network care; health maintenance organizations, or HMOs, generally do not cover nonemergency care outside their networks.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe premiums alone don't tell the whole story. Health policy research nonprofit\u0026nbsp;\u003ca href=\"https://www.kff.org/medicare/medicare-part-d-premiums-and-cost-sharing-in-2027/\"\u003eKFF projects\u003c/a\u003e \u0026nbsp;that the average premium for a stand-alone drug plan will rise from $34 a month in 2026 to $51 in 2027 for people who keep their existing plans. Costs vary by plan, and most beneficiaries must continue paying their Medicare Part B premium whether they choose original Medicare or Medicare Advantage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eBefore you enroll, check your doctors, prescriptions and out-of-pocket costs\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBefore enrolling in an Advantage plan, seniors should verify that their doctors and preferred hospitals accept the specific plan, Krantz said. Asking whether a doctor accepts insurance from a particular company isn't enough: A practice may take some of the company's plans but not others.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePrescription coverage warrants the same scrutiny. Plans cover different drugs and may charge different prices depending on the pharmacy.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBeneficiaries should also check prior authorization rules for care they expect to need, said Jeannie Fuglesten Biniek, deputy director of KFF's Program on Medicare Policy. Even extra benefits such as dental coverage can have important limits.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"There's a lot going on underneath the hood about benefits,\" Biniek said. \"A check on Plan Finder that says, ‘dental benefits,’ doesn't mean the same thing for every plan.\"\u003c/p\u003e \u003ca class=\"p-smartembed\" data-onecms-id=\"contentid/9ee2a160-c8f6-4475-bbad-efb1dc6980d4\" data-onecms-type=\"storywidget\" data-subtype=\"htmlBlurb\" href=\"javascript:window.parent.actionEventData({$contentId:'contentid/9ee2a160-c8f6-4475-bbad-efb1dc6980d4', $action:'view', $target:'work'})\" polopoly:contentid=\"contentid/9ee2a160-c8f6-4475-bbad-efb1dc6980d4\"\u003e\u003cspan\u003eSTORYWIDGET: BZMEDICARE-tipsgraphic\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/a\u003e \n\u003ch3\u003eWhy the right Medicare plan today may not be right next year\u003c/h3\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThere is no universally best plan, said Grace-Marie Horan, founder and CEO of insurance agency\u0026nbsp;Senior Health Plan Specialists Inc.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"People ask, ‘What’s the best [plan]?,’ but there is none,\" Horan said. \"It’s about what’s right for you, and that changes as your health changes.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eSuffolk County resident Ted Weber told Newsday he chose a $0-premium Medicare Advantage plan because he needs little medical care and found it cheaper than purchasing supplemental coverage.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eChelle Osleeb, also of Suffolk, switched from a Medicare supplemental plan with higher monthly premiums and a lower deductible to a cheaper plan when she had few medical needs. After being diagnosed with cancer, she switched back to the more expensive plan.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNew York makes such switches easier than most states: Medigap insurers must accept eligible applicants throughout the year without charging more based on health status, although some preexisting-condition waiting periods may apply.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eStill, many beneficiaries don't compare their options. Two-thirds of Medicare beneficiaries do not compare coverage options, KFF policy analyst Nancy Ochieng said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I don't think it's intended to set it and forget it,\" Biniek said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBeneficiaries can compare plans at Medicare.gov or get free, unbiased counseling through New York's Health Insurance Information, Counseling and Assistance Program at 800-701-0501.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMedicare's annual open enrollment period ends Dec. 7, with coverage changes taking effect Jan. 1.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/cd25147a-d66f-4d66-8211-521c119bae0f","title":"AIAudio - 33,000 Long Islanders losing Medicare plans for 2027.
