$218.3 million spending plan for next year. The tax levy will increase nearly 5.8% from $148.3 million in this year’s budget to $156.9 million for 2027. The average resident not living in a village will see a $113 annual increase in taxes.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTown officials said $75 of that $113 is due to increased costs for health insurance and pension payouts, as well as salary increases for\u0026nbsp;contracted union employees.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAfter facing \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/schaffer-babylon-budget-tax-increase-raise-ewed2gbv\"\u003efierce criticism from residents\u003c/a\u003e\u0026nbsp;over a proposed 29% — or $36,320 — increase in his salary \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/babylon-town-proposed-budget-oempokc3\"\u003ein the new budget\u003c/a\u003e, Supervisor Rich Schaffer last week announced to Newsday that he would \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/towns/babylon-supervisor-schaffer-pay-cut-cuctkx9v\"\u003eforgo forego the raise\u003c/a\u003e and instead take a pay cut from $123,680 to $120,000.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe town also removed salary increases for other elected officials that had been included in the budget, including a 13.3% raise for Tax Receiver Jennifer Montiglio and a 9.7% bump for Town Clerk Janina Martinez, which would have brought both of their pay to $140,000. The original proposed budget also included a 4.8% increase for the four town council members to a collective $315,000 salary.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThose savings did little to chip away at the tax levy increase, however, and the town’s new budget busts the state’s 2% tax cap. In response to public reproach for piercing the tax cap for the fourth time in five years, the town has promised the budgets for 2028 and 2029 will stay under the cap.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePrior to the board vote on Wednesday, just over a half dozen residents expressed their frustration with the tax hike, saying yearly increases may force them to live elsewhere.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Why not look at reducing nonessential spending, improve efficiency, spending reduction taken from reserves and seek alternative revenue,\" Deer Park resident Sherry Levinson said. \"We want to stay in Deer Park so we are trying to keep ourselves in our homes by living within our means. We would like you to find additional savings by carefully and thoughtfully reviewing line by line the expenses.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMany also criticized the budget process, with several residents asking the town to move such meetings to the evening and to have a forum that would allow residents to have specific budget questions answered.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I think that the town needs to be more responsive to your constituents,\" Elise Antonelli, of Babylon, told the board, adding a request that the town create an advisory board where residents can \"give you our input and actually have a dialogue with you.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAsked by Newsday after the meeting whether the process might change next year, town officials said they would consider adjustments.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We've heard the requests for evening meetings and budget workshops, and that feedback is part of how we'll look at the way we conduct business going forward,\" town spokesman Ryan Bonner said in a statement. \"Every Town Board meeting is streamed live on YouTube, and anyone who can't attend in person can submit comments online and get a response.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAntonelli told Newsday after the meeting that she had sent budget questions to the town but the answers were unsatisfactory. petition filed with the Nassau County Surrogate's Court, one of the couple's two sons, who also is listed as part owner of the Maria Lane home, said his father, Peishun Fan, 48, at the time of his disappearance, had accumulated assets, including bank accounts, of $12 million, as well as others still unknown.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eFan and his wife, Juanjuan Zhang, 44, were reported missing on March 31, 2025. Since then and despite searches by the Nassau County Police Department, FBI and family members, both in the United States and China, there's been no trace of the couple. They immigrated to the United States in 2022 with their two sons, Yiwei Fan, now 21, and his brother, now 13. Both sons lived with their parents in the home, which was purchased for $3.8 million in cash in late 2023 by Yiwei Fan and his mother. Neither the sons nor anyone else has communicated with the couple in the past 18 months.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe court is being asked to appoint temporary administrators because the property is falling behind on payments like taxes and utility bills, and the younger son's needs must be addressed, records showed.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eVarious property expenses \"have not been paid since [Peishun Fan] disappeared and the other monthly financial obligations ... including the maintenance and support of his minor son,\" court records stated.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eLegal proceedings were started in May in the surrogate's court for the appointment of the fiduciaries.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/nassau/sons-return-china-missing-couple-a8ppckid\"\u003eBoth sons\u003c/a\u003e are currently in China and are having trouble getting visas to return to the United States because their missing mother was listed as their sponsor, said attorney John Carman, who has represented Yiwei Fan and his younger brother in legal proceedings since their parents disappeared.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCarman and a retired NYPD officer named Baimadajie Angwang, who is also a private investigator, are being recommended by Yiwei Fan to serve with him as co-administrators. Nassau Surrogate David P. Sullivan has yet to sign an order appointing the administrators, court records showed.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCarman didn't return phone calls and text messages from Newsday on Thursday seeking comment. Angwang couldn't be reached for comment.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe case of the missing couple has puzzled their neighbors and also has been a topic of discussion in the local Chinese American community. One neighbor told Newsday that in recent days, cars have shown up at the house and some young people entered, stayed a short while and left. Lights are left on, but the landscaping is overgrown.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"It is very distressing,\" said the neighbor, who didn't want to be identified.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDet. Joe Oginski of the Nassau County Police Department told Newsday on Thursday that a missing person\u0026nbsp;investigation into the couple's disappearance remains active and ongoing. Anyone with information should contact the department's Missing Persons\u0026nbsp;squad at 516-573-7347.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAmong the mysteries surrounding the case is how the couple made their money. Earlier, Carman said Peishun Fan had a construction business in China years ago but had some legal problems that led to a brief period of incarceration there.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWhen Zhang applied for immigration status to the United States, she applied for a special business visa, apparently to do real estate, but it was unclear if that venture ever got off the ground, Carman noted months ago.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/crime/long-island-missing-couple-sentencing-wu-n1j09cnb\"\u003eEarlier this year\u003c/a\u003e, a Queens woman, Qiuju Wu, 58, pleaded guilty to federal charges that she stole $2.8 million from the missing couple. Prosecutors believe Wu's crime was identity theft and had nothing to do with the disappearances of Fan and Zhang. As part of her plea, Wu was ordered to pay the government $1.8 million in restitution and forfeit another $1 million.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn describing the family situation before his parents disappeared, Yiwei Fan said in the court papers that life was good.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Peishun Fan is happily married to ... Juanjuan Zhang and enjoyed being a father,\" he said in court papers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAs far as being aware of any reason for the parents' sudden and mysterious disappearance, Yiwei Fan said he knew of none.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/010bdce0-1201-4384-ab81-0df98ac1c1b2","title":"AIAudio - witnesses in the case, records indicate.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003ePhilip Masorti, Abbatiello's attorney, said that in granting $250,000 bail for his client, the judge had rejected the Fitch CEO Michael Jeffries appeared \"confused,\" had a \"shuffling gait\" and tremors during a 2023 cognitive assessment that resulted in a diagnosis of dementia, a clinical neuropsychologist testified Tuesday at a pretrial hearing to determine Jeffries' mental fitness to stand trial on charges he sex trafficked victims.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJacqueline C. Valdes testified for Jeffries' defense that she twice assessed him — in 2023 and earlier this year — and agreed with another doctor's opinion that he had a major neurocognitive disorder.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"There was evidence in 2023 of cognitive impairments ... and he was confused,\" Valdes said, which included issues with learning, memory, executive functions and problems with \"shifting gears.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eValdes also noted he has physical \"abnormalities\" that she said relate to a \"shuffling gait,\" had difficulty rising from a chair and had tremors.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJeffries was also \"acting out his dreams,\" Valdes said and was experiencing hallucinations and \"some delusional thinking.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHe was once found \"sitting in the next door neighbor's yard in his underwear,\" Valdes said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJeffries, 81, of West Palm Beach, Florida, attended Tuesday's hearing in federal court in Central Islip. The former CEO, with thick white hair and clad in a suit, sat at the defense table with his lawyers and did not appear to visibly react to the testimony. His adult son sat in the first row of spectators.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJeffries, who was initially deemed unfit to stand trial, was found to be competent after a monthslong , court-ordered evaluation at the Federal Medical Center in Butner, North Carolina,\u0026nbsp; last year. But his lawyers disagreed.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eValdes said there was evidence that Jeffries' condition had begun in 2013, when an MRI showed \"mild atrophy,\" or a shrinking of the brain.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eA 2018 brain scan, taken after Jeffries fell in South Africa and experienced a traumatic injury that induced bleeding of the brain, also showed atrophy, Valdes said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAt the time of the fall, doctors had \"concerns\" about Jeffries' alcohol use, as he was drinking in the hospital, according to medical records, Valdes said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut later testing showed his liver was functioning normally and he did not appear to have alcohol-related dementia.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn 2025, doctors diagnosed Jeffries with major neurocognitive disorder, or dementia, probable Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia, Valdes said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHer testimony comes on the first day of a pretrial hearing to help U.S. District Judge Nusrat J. Choudhury determine whether Jeffries will stand trial later this year.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJeffries has pleaded not guilty to federal charges of sex trafficking and interstate prostitution.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutors say Jeffries, his romantic partner and a third man used the promise of modeling jobs to lure men to drug-fueled sex parties in New York City, the Hamptons and other locations. The charges echoed sexual misconduct accusations made in a civil case and the media in recent years.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eJeffries left Abercrombie in 2014 after more than two decades at the helm. His partner, Matthew Smith, has also pleaded not guilty and remains free on bond, as has their co-defendant, James Jacobson.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eUnder direct questioning from Jeffries' defense attorney Brian Bieber, Valdes confirmed Jeffries had told prison staff when he was confined in North Carolina \"he hoped to be found incompetent.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eValdes said that was another example of \"uninhibited behavior\" from Jeffries, also another dementia symptom.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eProsecutor Adam Toporovsky pointed out to Valdes that some of Jeffries' results of cognitive testing improved when she examined him this year from the 2023 results.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut Valdes attributed any improvements to the likelihood his prescribed medication, Seroquel, was working.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe hearing continues Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e","textAudio":{"id":"contentid/8981acd1-b213-4a1b-8a10-22f96100e6ae","title":"AIAudio - Ferrara","organization":"Newsday","floatLeft":false,"floatRight":false,"imageSize":"","useFreeform":false},"content":{"__typename":"Article","id":"contentid/d0cc2deb-4eb8-4e13-b184-4b440e08b5f2","lead":"Some bus stops remained buried in snow two weeks after a January storm.","body":"\u003cp\u003eA pair of winter storms earlier this year exposed delays in clearing snow around some bus stops, leading to unsafe conditions for travelers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eTo avoid similar problems when the next big snowstorm hits, Suffolk County is seeking to get a\u0026nbsp;contract\u0026nbsp;in place with a snow removal company\u0026nbsp;that can quickly respond to clear snow from the 136 county-owned bus shelters.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eBut fast-tracking the contract got held up by administrative hurdles on Wednesday.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eNewsday \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/bus-stops-snow-nice-bus-suffolk-transit-bi5ldfzi\" target=\"_blank\"\u003ereported earlier this year\u003c/a\u003e that some bus stops in both Nassau and Suffolk remained buried in snow two weeks after a January storm. An \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/news/weather/weather-wintry-mix-long-island-khcadrfz\" target=\"_blank\"\u003eeven larger blizzard\u003c/a\u003e followed in February with as much as 31 inches of snow.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCounty officials say they don't have the crew to reasonably\u0026nbsp;dig out the bus shelters, 2,249 bus stops and six major transfer locations if a major storm hits. The county — which experienced several walloping snowstorms resulting in the declaration of at least two state of emergencies\u0026nbsp;— is seeking bids\u0026nbsp;through its Office of Central Procurement for a requirements contract for companies that can deliver the as-needed service.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"With Suffolk County bus ridership increasing it has become even more critical to address any major snowfall on our bus stops and shelters,\" Suffolk County Executive Edward P. Romaine said in a statement.\u0026nbsp;\"These kind of agreements allow us to work quickly and not waste time keeping people safe.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe county's Department of Economic Development and Planning sought a waiver on Wednesday to enter into contracts with two companies that were previously used on an emergency basis. The waiver would have allowed the county to have the companies in place before the bidding process is complete, in the event of a December storm.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe RFP Waiver Committee, which approves contracts that bypass the county's traditional competitive procurement process, tabled the resolution.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eWilliam Duffy, counsel to the legislature, said the department needs to find another avenue to enter into a temporary agreement since it's a public works contract that doesn't fall under what the waiver\u0026nbsp;committee can approve.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"I'm not questioning whether this is a good contract or not,\" Duffy said during the meeting. \"I just don't think we have the ability to approve it.\"\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eElisa Picca, chief transportation officer, said at the meeting the county likely won't have the requirements contract in place for another six to eight weeks, leaving a gap in December.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eDuffy suggested they speak to the county attorney to find a solution.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eMike Martino, spokesman for Romaine, told Newsday earlier this year that there are an additional 166 bus stops with shelters that the county does not own and clearing snow from those locations is not county responsibility.\u003c/p\u003e","publishedDate":"2026-11-18T21:03:38.847Z","updatedDate":"2026-11-19T00:29:33.274Z","url":"https://www.newsday.com/long-island/politics/suffolk-snow-contract-dz06v1tg","headline":"Suffolk seeks to fast-track snow removal contract at bus stops after complaints","teaserTitle":"Suffolk seeks to fast-track snow removal contract after complaints","newsLabel":"none","newsLabel2":"none","subType":"article","disableDeepLink":false,"moveAd":false,"textAudio":{"id":"contentid/b0ae6548-4da2-4bf9-b323-c13208ac2fb4","title":"AIAudio - A Newsday reporter confirmed that 7-Eleven signage had replaced, or partly replaced, with QuickChek branding at all former locations except for Bohemia.\u0026nbsp;\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e7-Eleven has applied to the New York State Liquor Authority to sell beer at all locations, with an active license at the Brentwood location, and conditional approvals issued for Copiague\u0026nbsp;and Commack. The applications for Bohemia, Lake Grove and Bethpage are still under review.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eQuickChek opened its first convenience store on Long Island in 2014, \u003ca href=\"https://www.newsday.com/business/quickchek-bohemia-convenience-store-n00909\"\u003eNewsday has reported\u003c/a\u003e, and operates dozens of stores throughout New Jersey and the Hudson Valley. The Whitehouse, New Jersey-based chain is owned by parent company Murphy USA, a gasoline retailer.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eIn \u003ca href=\"https://s22.q4cdn.com/506259022/files/content_files/MurphyUSA_Q3_2026_Q_A_Transcript.pdf\"\u003ean earnings call on Oct. 29\u003c/a\u003e, company CEO Malynda West said QuickChek is facing pressure\u0026nbsp;as a \"food forward model\" that costs more to run.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"We're remaining focused on improving our merchandise performance through things like sharper pricing, right assortment, executing well on our food and beverage capability. We're also working on the cost side of our business, tightly aligning the labor and our operating costs to the actual customer demand that we're seeing,\" she said.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e7-Eleven has not yet posted third-quarter results, but in 2025, outlined for investors \u003ca href=\"https://www.7andi.com/en/ir/file/library/ks/pdf/2025_0806kse_01.pdf\"\u003ea planned \"transformation\"\u003c/a\u003e of the company.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eThe Irving, Texas-based chain noted challenges including cost-push inflation, shifts in consumer spending, franchisee profitability, declining fuel demand and intensifying competition.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAddressing these challenges includes\u0026nbsp;plans to invest in stronger food offerings at thousands of locations and accelerating store expansion even as \"competitors slow down,\" according to the presentation.\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eHaving more stores in an area can improve efficiencies in terms of labor, marketing and labor, said Jeff Lenard, a spokesman for NACS, a global trade association for convenience and fuel retailers.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eAffordability has been a challenge for retailers and consumers, he added,\u0026nbsp;noting that customer visits to convenience stores were down around 4% in the first half of 2026.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eCustomers did spend more\u0026nbsp;during those visits, but that was partially because of higher prices, he said.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003eConcerns about inflated costs may be limiting impulse purchases\u0026nbsp;from consumers fresh off filling their gas tanks, who might have otherwise purchased something from a convenience store, Lenard added.\u003c/p\u003e \n\u003cp\u003e\"Prices have been higher, gas prices have been significantly higher until of late, and they're still elevated. Everybody's looking for ways to attract and keep customers,\" he said.\u003c/p\u003e","publishedDate":"2026-11-18T18:38:52.541Z","updatedDate":"2026-11-19T01:05:45.240Z","url":"https://www.newsday.com/business/quickchek-7-eleven-c4yblgmd","headline":"QuickChek's Long Island locations to be taken over by 7-Eleven","teaserTitle":"QuickChek's LI locations to be taken over by 7-Eleven","newsLabel":"none","newsLabel2":"none","subType":"article","disableDeepLink":false,"moveAd":false,"textAudio":{"id":"contentid/846f2f55-1c26-4d86-b08b-8d1cb8367849","title":"AIAudio - QuickChek's Long Island locations to be taken over by 7-Eleven\n","headline":"AIAudio - QuickChek's Long Island locations to be taken over by 7-Eleven","mediaLink":null,"premiumType":"inherit","url":"https://www.newsday.com/business/aiaudio-quickcheks-long-island-locations-to-be-taken-over-by-7-eleven-k1hk8h54","updatedDate":null,"publishedDate":null,"newsLabel":null,"audioUrl":"https://api.newsday.atexcloud.io//file-delivery-service/version/c:NDkyYjYyYzktNWI3NC00:ZmI5YWRhNmMtOWE4MS00/audio
